clinical_record:
A woman in her 60s presented with numerous whitish papules on the back of more than 10 years' duration. The lesions previously resolved with topical corticosteroids but flared soon after treatment discontinuation. Some papules became pruritic and extended to the waist and anterior trunk in the past month. No family history of similar lesions was recorded.

Multiple hypopigmented, flat-topped papules on the back, waist, and inframammary area without genital involvement. Most lesions were folliculocentric under close inspection. Dermoscopy revealed central keratin plugs and some foci of structureless, whitish, and homogenous areas with surrounding erythema.

- Laboratory tests: Antinuclear antibody and hyperglobulinemia tests were negative.- Histopathologic examination:   - Biopsy specimen from back showed central follicular plug and epidermal atrophy covered by orthokeratotic stratum corneum  - Papillary dermis was markedly thickened with homogenized collagens, areas of edema, and sparse bandlike lymphocytic infiltration  - Some eosinophils in infiltrate and red blood cell extravasation  - Congo red and mucicarmine stains were negative for amyloid and mucin- Images:  Image A Title: Clinical presentation  Image A Description: Multiple hypopigmented, atrophic, keratotic, and folliculocentric papules on the trunk    Image B Title: Dermoscopic findings  Image B Description: Two foci of central keratin plugs and another ill-defined, whitish, and homogenous area with surrounding erythema    Image C Title: Histopathologic examination  Image C Description: Biopsy specimen (hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×100)

What is the most likely diagnosis?

reviewer_a.decisive_span: Papillary dermis was markedly thickened with homogenized collagens, areas of edema, and sparse bandlike lymphocytic infiltration
reviewer_a.reason: Lichen spinulosus is characterized by grouped follicular papules with a central keratotic spine, but the histopathology of homogenized collagen and epidermal atrophy seen in the record is not consistent with lichen spinulosus.

reviewer_b.decisive_span: central follicular plug and epidermal atrophy
reviewer_b.missing_or_conflicting_component: Lichen spinulosus lacks the homogenized collagen and epidermal atrophy characteristic of lichen sclerosus.
reviewer_b.reason: Lichen spinulosus is a distinct follicular keratosis without the dermal sclerosis and atrophy seen in this case.

clinical_record:
A young black woman with sickle cell disease (HbSS variant) presented with a 2-day history of visual loss in the left eye. No dehydration or other precipitating factors were noted.

Visual acuity was 20/20 OD and 20/800 OS. Right eye examination was unremarkable except for peripheral retinal black sunburst lesions. In her left eye, ischemic macular whitening was noted. No cherry-red spot, hemorrhage, or peripheral neovascularization was present.

- Fluorescein angiography (left eye): Normal cilioretinal, retinal arteriolar, and retinal venous filling; abnormal retinal capillary bed across the macula, with increased intercapillary spacing and small areas of hypofluorescence nasal to the fovea.- OCT (left eye): Hyperreflective plaques at the level of the INL/OPL, corresponding to ophthalmoscopically opaque areas. OCT Collage Image  Image Description: Foveal scan at outcome vs scan of healthy age-matched person, demonstrating atrophy of middle retinal layers- OCT (right eye): Temporal macular thinning.

clinical_record:
A 55-year-old white woman with a history of diverticulosis and colonic polyps presented with new-onset flulike symptoms followed by low-grade fever, facial crusted plaques, and 4 weeks of bloody and watery diarrhea. Her facial lesions initially presented as ill-defined pink patches over her cheeks and red papules on her forehead. Over the next 4 days, the lesions spread to her chest, abdomen, back, and left buttock, and a single papule appeared on the right lower extremity. Her low-grade fevers and diarrhea persisted throughout this 4-day period.

In the emergency department, she was febrile and tachycardic. Physical findings included:- 6 × 7-cm well-demarcated vegetative crusted plaques on the bilateral cheeks- Several discrete, round, 1- to 2-cm crusted plaques on the temple- Discrete pustules, vesicles, and umbilicated papules on cheeks and temple- Lesions on chest, abdomen, back, and left buttock- Painful subcutaneous nodules over lower extremities- Polyarthralgia

Laboratory Tests:- Mild leukocytosis with normal differential- Mildly elevated transaminase and alkaline phosphatase levels- Negative wound culture- Blood cultures showed no growth- Negative PCR for herpes simplex virus- Negative direct fluorescent antibody assay for varicella-zoster virusPathology:- Forehead lesion biopsy: Intradermal neutrophilic inflammation with ulceration and intracorneal neutrophils. Special stains negative for microorganisms- Right thigh biopsy: Septal panniculitis with Miescher radial granulomas- Colonoscopy: Moderate inflammation, edema, erosions, and pseudopolyps in the sigmoid colonImages:Image 1 Title: Clinical Appearance of Facial Neutrophilic DermatosisImage 1 Description: A, A 6 × 7-cm, well-demarcated, vegetative crusted plaque on the left cheek and a discrete, round, 1- to 2-cm crusted plaque on the foreheadImage 2 Title: Histopathological Findings of Facial Neutrophilic DermatosisImage 2 Description: Shave biopsy specimen from forehead lesion showing diffuse intradermal neutrophilic infiltrate with central ulceration

What is the most likely diagnosis?
reference_diagnosis: IBD-associated neutrophilic dermatosis with ulcerative colitis

reviewer_a.decisive_span: vegetative crusted plaques on the bilateral cheeks
reviewer_a.reason: Pyoderma gangrenosum is another type of neutrophilic dermatosis that can be associated with IBD, but the described lesions (crusted plaques, pustules, vesicles, umbilicated papules) and histopathology (intradermal neutrophilic inflammation with ulceration and intracorneal neutrophils) are more consistent with Sweet's syndrome, which is a specific type of neutrophilic dermatosis. Pyoderma gangrenosum typically presents with rapidly enlarging, painful ulcers with undermined violaceous borders.

reviewer_b.decisive_span: Septal panniculitis with Miescher radial granulomas
reviewer_b.missing_or_conflicting_component: Pyoderma gangrenosum is a different neutrophilic dermatosis with distinct clinical features; the histopathology here is classic for Sweet syndrome, not pyoderma gangrenosum.
reviewer_b.reason: Pyoderma gangrenosum is a related neutrophilic dermatosis but has a different clinical presentation and histopathology; the record supports Sweet syndrome, not pyoderma gangrenosum.

The patient had a 3-year history of hypertension but no history of neurological disorders. The patient was alert and oriented.

- Effacement of the right frontal wrinkle- Incomplete closure of the right eyelid- Flattening of the right nasolabial fold- Muscle strength in the right upper and lower extremities: grade 0/5- Hypoesthesia noted on the right side- Right Babinski sign: positive

- Imaging Studies:  1. Emergency CT scan of the head:     Image Title: Cranial computed tomography     Image Description: Hemorrhage in the left thalamus-radiation crown region and in the lateral ventricle at 24 hours postonset    2. Cerebral MRI with susceptibility-weighted imaging (1 week and 1 month after onset):     Image Description: No definitive lesions in the brainstem or evidence of hemorrhage-related iron deposition in the ventral part of the pons    3. Cerebral MRI with diffusion tensor imaging (1 month after onset):     Image Description: Corticobulbar tract appeared thinner on the left side than on the right before entering the brainstem

A 30-year-old woman presented with a large unhealed ulcer measuring 20 × 14-cm² that had persisted for the past 3 years. The patient had a patch of healthy skin (7.5 × 4 cm²) on her left forearm. Blood cell genotyping revealed compound heterozygous alterations (c.2992 + 2T>G and c.8621-30A>G) at splice sites in COL7A1.

The patient presented with:- A 20 × 14-cm² persistent ulcer on the back- A patch of healthy skin (7.5 × 4 cm²) on the left forearm, lacking blistering

1. Genetic Testing:- Blood cell genotyping showed compound heterozygous alterations in COL7A1- RNA transcript analysis using MinION platform:  * Affected skin epidermis: Dominant RNA transcripts with premature stop codons, wild-type reads rare (1.1%)  * Potentially revertant area epidermis: High rates of wild-type transcripts (35.0%)  * Revertant skin dermis: Wild-type reads rare (1.9%)2. Microscopy:- Immunofluorescence and transmission electron microscopy of the grafted area showed type VII collagen and anchoring fibrilsImages:- Figure 1A: Sanger sequencing showing compound heterozygous COL7A1 alteration- Figure 1B: Image of the persistent ulcer on patient's back- Figure 1C: Image of revertant skin patch on left forearm

What is the most likely diagnosis?
reference_diagnosis: Severe generalized recessive dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa (RDEB) with revertant mosaicism

reviewer_a.decisive_span: Blood cell genotyping revealed compound heterozygous alterations (c.2992 + 2T>G and c.8621-30A>G) at splice sites in COL7A1
reviewer_a.reason: This candidate identifies the core disease but misses the severity (severe generalized) and the specific genetic phenomenon (revertant mosaicism) which are crucial components of the reference diagnosis.

reviewer_b.decisive_span: compound heterozygous alterations ... in COL7A1
reviewer_b.missing_or_conflicting_component: recessive inheritance not explicitly stated
reviewer_b.reason: Correct disease family but lacks the recessive subtype and revertant mosaicism component.

clinical_record:
A woman in her 40s with a medical history of infective endocarditis and hepatitis C secondary to ongoing intravenous drug use presented to the emergency department with severe back pain. She had recently undergone tricuspid valve replacement with a 29-mm bioprosthetic Carpentier-Edwards valve complicated by transient third-degree heart block. Two days after pacemaker placement, she experienced episodes of light-headedness and chest pain.

Blood pressure was 94/60 mm Hg. Heart rates were between 150 and 190 beats per minute.

- Electrocardiogram findings:    Image Title: Figure 1. Electrocardiogram During Tachycardia    Image Description: Shows P waves upright in leads II, III, and aVF with sinus rate of 96 beats per minute. Grouped beating pattern with 1 P wave producing 2 QRS complexes, creating a regularly irregular rhythm.      - Prior Imaging:    Transesophageal echocardiography revealed pulmonic valve vegetations and severe tricuspid valve regurgitation secondary to a flail leaflet.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

reviewer_a.reason: Infective endocarditis is mentioned in the patient's history and as a cause of tricuspid valve issues, but it is not the primary diagnosis for the presenting symptoms of light-headedness, chest pain, and tachycardia.

reviewer_b.decisive_span: medical history of infective endocarditis
reviewer_b.reason: Infective endocarditis is the underlying predisposing condition but is not the arrhythmia diagnosis requested.

A patient in their 60s presented to the emergency department with approximately 20 minutes of acute, severe precordial chest pain radiating to their left arm at night, accompanied by dyspnea, dizziness, and sweating. The patient's medical history was notable for hypertension, cerebral infarction, diabetes, and nicotine addiction.

Vital signs showed blood pressure of 188/101 mm Hg, heart rate at 84 beats/min, and respiratory rate at 20 breaths/min.

- Laboratory tests:
  - Serum cardiac troponin I level: <0.05 ng/mL (normal range, <0.16 ng/mL)

  Image B Title: Post-procedural ECG
  Image B Description: Sinus rhythm at 65 beats/min with normalization of the T-wave morphology in leads V2 through V5

- Coronary angiography:
  Finding: Subtotal occlusion of the proximal left anterior descending artery

clinical_record:
A man in his 60s presented with a lesion on the left lower eyelid. His ocular history was notable for a traumatic icicle injury as a child that resulted in loss of the left eye. He had surgery to place an implant into the eye socket, and approximately 14 years prior underwent a lower eyelid reconstruction. He had excellent prosthesis position without need for refitting or replacement for more than 10 years until recently noting that his ocular prosthesis would spontaneously extrude from his anophthalmic socket.

On examination, he had a small, pearly lesion in the tear trough region of the left lower eyelid that had been growing over the past few months. He had contraction of the conjunctival mucosal tissue across the fornix of the left lower eyelid and increased scleral show of his ocular prosthesis with shortening of his lower eyelid skin. His prosthesis was extruded from his socket due to cicatricial effects causing conjunctival shrinkage and eyelid skin contracture.

- Imaging:  Image Title: Local Recurrence Within Electronic Surface Brachytherapy Field  Image Description: An elevated, pearly lesion on the left lower eyelid with scleral show on the prosthetic eye of the left lateral lower eyelid, showing conjunctival forniceal shortening with extrusion of the prosthesis and cicatricial shortening of the lower eyelid skin- Pathology:  Initial shave biopsy revealed nodular BCC of the left cheek  Subsequent biopsy specimen showed infiltrative pattern with no signs of fibrosis or inflammatory infiltrate

A female infant with history of acute lymphoblastic leukemia was admitted for reinduction chemotherapy. Seventeen days after her last day of chemotherapy, while neutropenic, she became febrile. Patient had an indwelling catheter.

A woman in her 60s presented with an itchy plaque on the mid-back. She had had a lesion at that site since childhood, which had remained asymptomatic and pea sized for most of that time. However, over the 10 years prior to presentation it had gradually increased in size and became itchy. There was also occasional oozing of serosanguineous fluid and bleeding from the lesion.

Examination revealed a 1.5 × 1.0-cm well-defined erythematous plaque with overlying ulceration on the mid-back, 1 cm left of the spine. Adjoining skin showed a horseshoe-shaped oval area of lichenification.

A woman in her 30s presented with asymptomatic erythematous scaly plaques over the face and proximal extremities. The lesions started as an erythematous papule on the face, progressing to larger plaques within 10 years. There was involvement of the upper respiratory tract, causing palatal perforation and stridor, necessitating a tracheostomy a year ago. History of wheezing and breathlessness. No history of preceding trauma, fever, malaise, joint pain, cough, epistaxis, hemoptysis, or hematuria.

Multiple well-defined brown erythematous scaly plaques with central scarring measuring 2 × 1 to 8 × 7 cm on the face, arm, and thighs. Saddle nose deformity, perforation of the hard palate, and necrotic plaques on the ear with destruction of ear cartilage. Cervical lymphadenopathy: multiple, nontender, discrete nodes, ranging from 1.5 to 2 cm without surface changes. Sensory examination and peripheral nerve examination within normal limits. Respiratory examination normal.

  - Kidney function test: normal
  - Liver function test: normal
  - Fasting blood glucose: normal
  - Urinalysis: normal

A White man in his 50s presented with painful oral erosions that began 2 years before. Medical history included recurrent respiratory infections and diarrhea. A previous intestinal biopsy had shown unspecific findings and absence of apoptosis. He reported a 5-kg weight loss attributed to impaired intake due to oral lesions. He was being evaluated for a mediastinal mass detected during chest radiography performed for pneumonia.

Physical examination revealed whitish edematous lacy patches with erosions on the dorsal and lateral aspects of the tongue and buccal mucosa. Skin and nails were not involved.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

reviewer_b.missing_or_conflicting_component: No immunodeficiency features included

Six hours prior, he had experienced similar chest pain at rest that resolved spontaneously after 30 minutes. Medical history included hypertension for 5 years, treated with reserpine.

Patient had diaphoresis and was in moderate distress. Vital signs: blood pressure 170/109 mm Hg, heart rate 87 beats per minute, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96% on room air. Jugular venous pressure was not elevated, lungs were clear. Heart sounds were regular and normal, without murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Other physical examination findings were unremarkable.

Initial serum troponin I level: 1.159 ng/mL (normal range ≤0.028 ng/mL)

- Sinus rhythm of 67 beats per minute
- Upsloping ST-segment depression leads V1 through V6
- Tall, symmetric T waves in leads V2 and V3
- 2-mm ST-segment elevation in avR
- Reciprocal ST-segment depression in leads II, III, and aVF

Second ECG (Figure B):
- Upsloping ST-segment depression in leads V3 through V6
- Biphasic T waves in leads V2 to V4

- Coronary Angiography:
Revealed 95% stenosis of the proximal left anterior descending artery

- Hypomotility in the anterior wall
- Left ventricular ejection fraction: 57%
- B-type natriuretic peptides were within normal range

clinical_record:
A man in his 60s presented with painful swelling of the proximal nail folds, dripping of blood from his fingernails and toenails for the last year, and occasional pus discharge. There was no history of preceding trauma or drug intake. Oral mucosa showed lichenoid plaques on the right angle of mouth, bilateral buccal mucosa, and erosions covered with hemorrhagic crusts on the upper and lower lips.

The proximal nail folds were found to be swollen and showed violaceous discoloration of 7 fingernails and 3 toenails. The index fingernails demonstrated longitudinal ridging, thinning, and focal fragmentation of the nail plate, while the remaining fingernails and involved toenails showed partial to complete loss of nail plate with oozing of blood resulting in hemorrhagic crusting of the nail beds and folds.

- Laboratory tests: Revealed raised liver enzyme levels and positive anti–hepatitis C virus antibody status.

- Histopathology:
Biopsy from proximal nail fold of right index finger showed:
- Hyperkeratosis
- Hypergranulosis
- Acanthosis
- Basal cell degeneration
- Numerous apoptotic keratinocytes in the epidermis
- Dense bandlike lymphohistiocytic infiltrate in the papillary dermis

Description: Shows hyperkeratosis, hypergranulosis, acanthosis, basal cell degeneration, Civatte bodies in the epidermis, and dense bandlike lymphohistiocytic infiltrate in the upper dermis

candidate_label: Primary cutaneous CD4+ small/medium T-cell lymphoma
clinical_record:
A man in his 70s presented with a persistent eruption of 5 years' duration. He had been treated with oral methotrexate for presumed chronic dermatitis after treatments with oral antibiotics, oral doxepin, and UV-B phototherapy had failed. Investigation of medical records revealed a history of HSV-2 infection on the buttocks prior to the development of the current eruption at the same site.

Multiple erythematous and violaceous plaques and nodules clustered on the superior buttocks and intergluteal cleft bilaterally. The lesions were smooth and firm.

clinical_record:
An 83-year-old woman presented with worsening left lower extremity pain, swelling, and erythema for the past few months. Previously independent in activities of daily living 2-3 months ago, she had become fully dependent on her daughter due to severe lower extremity pain. No history of trauma, recent travel, fever, chills, nausea, or vomiting. Medical history included stage I breast cancer in remission for 8 years after lumpectomy, radiation, and anastrozole therapy. Current medications included hydrochlorothiazide, gabapentin, montelukast, and albuterol. Former tobacco smoker. Had received radiation followed by immunotherapy, previously treated with nivolumab and sotorasib, and began new medication 3 months before presentation. Lower extremity erythema began a couple of weeks after first cycle, with last cycle given 3 weeks before current presentation.

Patient was afebrile and normotensive with normal heart rate. Bilateral lower extremities were hyperpigmented with significant pitting edema. Left lower extremity had erythematous, ill-defined, and extremely tender plaques from toes to knee. Right lower extremity had smaller indurated plaques on the posterior ankle. Crepitus, fluctuance, purulence, and ulcers were absent.

- Laboratory tests:
  - Hemoglobin: 89 g/L (reference range, 114–144 g/L)
  - Mean corpuscular volume: 100.7 fL (reference range, 79.4–94.8 fL)
  - C-reactive protein: 72.8 mg/L (reference range, <10.0 mg/L)
  - Folate: 35.5 nmol/L (reference range, >13.4 nmol/L)
  - Vitamin B12: 824.9 pmol/L (reference range, 132.8–764.3 pmol/L)

- Imaging studies:

  - Contrasted computed tomography angiogram run-off

  - Multiple venous Doppler ultrasonography studies

  - Chest radiograph: 8.1×6.4-cm mass in the right upper zone
  - Computed tomography of chest: lesion with paratracheal lymphadenopathy

The patient developed progressive renal failure with microscopic hematuria. He was on prophylactic penicillin, to which he was adherent. Ten days later, the patient returned with fatigue and chills.

Patient was afebrile, hypertensive to 185/104 mm Hg, and tachycardic to 122 beats/min. He appeared fatigued. Examination was otherwise unremarkable, without evidence of meningismus, rash, joint abnormalities, or genitourinary symptoms.

- Laboratory findings:    * Leukocytosis to 22.4×10⁹/L    * Lactatemia to 2.5 mmol/L    * Serum creatinine level of 312.1 μmol/L (3.53 mg/dL; baseline, 171.5 μmol/L [1.94 mg/dL])    * Peripheral blood cultures: 2/2 cultures grew Gram-negative cocci    - Microbiology:    * Blood culture speciation results positive

What is the most likely diagnosis?

reviewer_a.decisive_span: 2/2 cultures grew Gram-negative cocci
reviewer_a.reason: The record states 'Gram-negative cocci' and later 'Neisseria' for speciation, which conflicts with 'Pseudomonas aeruginosa'.

reviewer_b.decisive_span: Gram-negative cocci
reviewer_b.missing_or_conflicting_component: Pseudomonas is a Gram-negative rod, not cocci
reviewer_b.reason: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a Gram-negative rod, conflicting with the Gram-negative cocci morphology described.

clinical_record:
A 61-year-old man with a medical history of factor V Leiden mutation (discovered after an episode of abdominal venous thromboembolism), hypothyroidism, uncontrolled type 2 diabetes mellitus, and four transient ischemic attacks. The patient presented with memory impairment and behavioral changes - he could not state the reason for his office visit, had difficulty finding his way back to his car, and would forget why he went to grocery stores or how to return home. He had received anticoagulation with enoxaparin for a year previously. No recent medication changes were reported.

- Blood pressure: 160/100 mm Hg- Mental status: Oriented to place and person- Neurological: Decreased sensation to touch and pinprick on bilateral upper and lower extremities and face

clinical_record:
A 63-year-old woman presented with difficult-to-treat hypertension. Medical history included bone and central diabetes insipidus diagnosed via femoral biopsy 12 years ago, and liver involvement three years prior that was treated with cytarabine for one year. The patient had untreated dyslipidemia (LDL cholesterol 3.11 mmol/L). She was not a smoker and did not have diabetes. Her body mass index was 19.22 kg/m². No relevant family history was reported. The patient did not report angina, exertional dyspnea, or claudication.

Blood pressure was 198/106 mmHg without orthostatic hypotension or anisosphygmia, and heart rate was 65 beats/min. The cardiopulmonary examination was unremarkable, and a continuous murmur was heard in the epigastric region.

- Laboratory Tests:    * Serum creatinine: 96.36 μmol/L (1.09 mg/dL)    * Potassium: 4.4 mmol/L    * B-type natriuretic peptide: 82,500 pg/mL    * Inflammatory markers: normal    * Urinalysis: unremarkable without albuminuria  - Imaging Studies:    * Transthoracic echocardiogram: left ventricular mass index of 110 g/m² without other relevant changes    * Abdominal CT angiogram:      Title: Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT      Description: Right kidney atrophy without discernible right renal artery and high-grade ostial stenosis of the left renal, celiac trunk, and superior mesenteric arteries    * Diethylenetriamine pentaacetate renogram: confirmed right kidney functional exclusion    * Renal vein catheterization: no signs of renin production lateralization

What is the most likely diagnosis?
reference_diagnosis: Mixed Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) and Erdheim-Chester disease (ECD) with renovascular hypertension

reviewer_a.reason: Takayasu arteritis is a large vessel vasculitis, typically affecting the aorta and its major branches. While it can cause renal artery stenosis, the clinical picture (age, specific imaging findings of ostial stenosis and atrophy) does not strongly point to Takayasu arteritis, and there are no other features like constitutional symptoms or differential blood pressures in the limbs that would suggest it over other causes of renovascular hypertension.

reviewer_b.decisive_span: bone and central diabetes insipidus diagnosed via femoral biopsy 12 years ago
reviewer_b.missing_or_conflicting_component: Takayasu arteritis is a large-vessel vasculitis; no evidence of vascular inflammation or typical demographic
reviewer_b.reason: The clinical picture is more consistent with histiocytosis with secondary renovascular hypertension, not Takayasu arteritis.

clinical_record:
A 61-year-old woman presented with worsening dyspnea over the previous six months, with acute exacerbation. Symptoms included dyspnea on exertion, 2-pillow orthopnea, fatigue, dry cough, and bilateral lower limb swelling worse in evenings. One episode of lightheadedness occurred a week before presentation. Medical history included a 20-year history of autoimmune condition with joint involvement, complicated by usual interstitial pneumonia pattern interstitial lung disease four years prior and keratoconjunctivitis sicca. Patient had poor therapeutic adherence due to significant barriers to care. Previous surgeries included tonsillectomy and partial hysterectomy. Non-smoker, no alcohol use.

Vital signs: BP 138/86 mmHg, pulse 85/min, temperature 96.5°F (35.8°C), BMI 16.3 kg/m², respiratory rate 20/min, oxygen saturation 93% on 3L oxygen. Patient was alert but chronically ill-looking and cachectic. Normal breath sounds on auscultation, no increased work of breathing or accessory muscle use. No jugular venous distention, normal heart sounds. Pupils equal and reactive, no conjunctival injection or scleral icterus. No skin rashes, ulcerations, palpable purpura, or nodules. No palpable lymph nodes. Abdomen soft, nontender, nondistended with normal bowel sounds. Muscle tone normal, power 5/5, no cranial nerve deficits. Bilateral ulnar deviation at metacarpophalangeal joints with swan neck deformities at third and fourth fingers bilaterally. No joint swelling, warmth, or redness, but tenderness noted.

Laboratory Tests:- Serum sodium: 123 mmol/L (Day 1), 136 mmol/L (Day 9)- Total protein: 116 g/L (Day 1), 69 g/L (Day 9)- Serum albumin: 41 g/L (Day 1), 40 g/L (Day 9)- Serum globulin: 21 g/L- Serum creatinine: <33.6 μmol/L- Complement C3: 0.79 g/L- Complement C4: 0.114 mg/L- Serum viscosity: 13.7 relative to H₂O (Day 1), 2.2 (Day 9)- Rheumatoid factor: >1000 kIU/L (Day 1), 464 kIU/L (Day 9)Imaging Studies:- CT angiography chest: showed pulmonary edema, no pulmonary embolism- Echocardiogram: left ventricular ejection fraction 45-50%Additional Tests:- Serum protein electrophoresis: no monoclonal protein spike- Ultrasound-guided abdominal fat pad biopsy: negative for amyloid

What is the most likely diagnosis?

reviewer_a.decisive_span: Echocardiogram: left ventricular ejection fraction 45-50%
reviewer_a.reason: Heart failure is a manifestation of the patient's condition (reduced LVEF, pulmonary edema, dyspnea) but not the overarching diagnosis of hyperviscosity syndrome in RA.

reviewer_b.decisive_span: CT angiography chest: showed pulmonary edema
reviewer_b.missing_or_conflicting_component: heart failure is a manifestation/sequela of hyperviscosity, not the underlying cause
reviewer_b.reason: Heart failure is a clinical consequence of hyperviscosity syndrome; the primary diagnosis is hyperviscosity syndrome.

A 45-year-old Filipino woman presented with a 2-day history of right-sided headache and emesis of clear fluid. She reported dizziness and generalized weakness but did not report chills, rigor, neck pain, unilateral limb weakness, or sensory loss. Right mastoid region showed a small gaping mastoidectomy wound with a small amount of greenish discharge. Otoscopy revealed greenish discharge in the right external auditory canal. Tympanic membrane was intact. Funduscopy showed no papilledema.

A 54-year-old woman living in upstate New York with a medical history significant for idiopathic CD4 lymphocytopenia (ICL) originally diagnosed in 2015 with an annual CD4 cell count ranging between 14 and 18 cells/µL. She initially presented to her primary care physician with a sore throat. When symptoms did not improve after one week, she was referred to an otolaryngologist. The sore throat persisted despite a trial of omeprazole and fluctuated in intensity over the following months. Several months later, the patient began to experience dysphonia along with odynophagia. Throughout this course, the patient had no systemic symptoms (fever, weight loss, myalgias) or pulmonary symptoms.

Laryngoscopy revealed thickening of the epiglottic mucosa with irregularity and white plaques. A repeat laryngoscopy demonstrated progression of the plaques.

  * Urine histoplasma antigen: positive at 0.3 ng/mL
  * Acid-fast stain and culture: negative

- Imaging Studies:
  * Computed tomography of the chest revealed subtle ground-glass opacities in the left upper lobe

- Pathological Examination:
  * Laryngeal biopsy revealed rare hyphae and yeast forms on Grocott methenamine silver stain with no evidence of malignancy or granulomas
  * Fungal culture grew Histoplasma capsulatum, identified by typical tuberculate microconidia

  * Figure 2 Title: Microscopy findings
  * Figure 2 Description: (A) Mold with cottony texture and white-tan reverse after 16 days incubation, (B) Lactophenol cotton blue tease mount preparation showing large, thick-walled, round tuberculate macroconidia at 400× magnification

clinical_record:
A 67-year-old female presented with three-year history of worsening dysarthria and dysphagia, choking episodes provoked when lying supine, a one-year history of constant pain at right occipital and cervical paraspinal areas and a 20-pound weight loss. She reported a distant one-year history of smoking with no alcohol or illicit drug use.

There was right tongue deviation, atrophy of the right side of her tongue, limited tongue movements and difficulty with tongue protrusion, but no tongue fasciculation. She had lingual and palatal dysarthria, and slow, but symmetric palate elevation. The rest of her neurological exam, including muscle and facial strength and reflexes, was unremarkable.

- Laboratory tests: Acetylcholine receptor antibodies, TSH, B12, ANA, ESR, and CK were normal.- EMG findings: Active denervation changes in the left lower lumbar paraspinals and medial gastrocnemius muscle, and minimal active denervation in the left first dorsal interosseous and pronator teres.- Imaging Studies:  1. MRI of the nasopharynx     Image Description: Shows infiltrative process at the base and root of the tongue, invading the most inferior aspects of the mouth floor, including the lingual neurovascular bundles    2. Maxillofacial CT     Image Description: Shows an enhancing, infiltrative, and partially necrotic mass of the floor of her mouth, centered on the left side and involving the midline, measuring 17 × 35 × 21 mm. Infiltration of the intrinsic tongue muscles with tongue atrophy.    3. Flexible laryngoscopy: Shows base of tongue fullness with prominent lymphatic tissue  - Pathology:  Biopsy results: Focal, non-keratinizing invasive squamous cell carcinoma  Additional findings: P16– INK and Cyto5/6 immunohistochemistry were positive

clinical_record:
A 29-year-old primigravida woman at 41+2 weeks of pregnancy. No history of gestational diabetes mellitus, preeclampsia, or coagulation disorders, and no anti-coagulation therapy with heparin. Initially admitted for transvaginal delivery, later requiring emergency cesarean section due to amniotic fluid turbidity. Intraoperative blood loss was 400 mL.

15 hours post-procedure: Right lower limb showed full recovery of sensation and muscle strength. Left lower limb showed mild soreness and swelling with manual muscle testing (MMT) grade of 2. At 45.5 hours post-procedure: Hypesthesia below chest level developed, followed by reduction in muscle strength of both lower limbs, progressing to flaccid paralysis.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

clinical_record:
A woman in her 50s presented with a 3-month history of rapidly spreading intensively pruritic papules on her extremities. The patient had no remarkable medical or family history and was not concurrently being treated with any medications. She had been previously treated with topical steroid ointments and oral compound glycyrrhizin tablets, which had no obvious effect.

The lesions consisted of scattered, erythematous, annular papules measuring up to 5 mm wide. Further examination revealed a few asymptomatic brown flat papules scattered on her face. The palms, soles, and oral mucosa were not involved.

- Laboratory tests: Routine blood, liver and kidney function, antistreptolysin O, C-reactive protein, antinuclear antibody, and rheumatoid factor tests disclosed no abnormal findings.- Histopathology:   Skin biopsy revealed:  - Mild hyperkeratosis accompanied by parakeratosis  - Atrophy of the epidermis  - Well-developed cornoid lamellae with a decreased granular layer  - Individual cell dyskeratosis  - Vacuolar degeneration of the basal cell layer  - Slight infiltrate of lymphocytes, histiocytes, and eosinophils in the upper dermis- Images:  Image 1 Title: Clinical images of keratotic papules  Image Description: Keratotic papules diffusely distributed on an extremity, shown in original and magnified views  Image 2 Title: Histologic findings (H&E stain)  Image Description: Shows skin hyperkeratosis accompanied by parakeratosis with an inflammatory infiltrate in the upper dermis, and at higher magnification, revealing lymphocytes, histiocytes, and eosinophils in the infiltrate

What is the most likely diagnosis?

reviewer_a.decisive_span: Well-developed cornoid lamellae
reviewer_a.reason: Grover's disease (transient acantholytic dermatosis) has distinct histopathological features, primarily acantholysis, which are not described here. The presence of cornoid lamellae points away from Grover's disease.

reviewer_b.decisive_span: Well-developed cornoid lamellae with a decreased granular layer
reviewer_b.reason: Grover's disease is a different entity; the histopathology is not consistent with porokeratosis.

A woman in her 30s presented with a painful bruise on her hand that initially appeared a few days after she sustained a twisting injury to the affected hand while participating in acroyoga 2 years before. Since the initial onset, the bruise and pain had persisted despite icing and resting the area. She denied any personal or family history of bleeding disorders.

An ill-defined indurated blue-green plaque was noted on the dorsum of the left hand.

- Radiography: Showed soft tissue swelling but were otherwise unremarkable.- Magnetic Resonance Imaging: Showed a heterogeneously fluid hyperintense and T1 heterogeneously hyperintense lesion measuring approximately 1.6 × 0.5 × 2.9 cm that was centered within the dorsal subcutaneous soft tissue of the hand.- Pathology:   - Mixed fibrous and mature adipose tissue with extensive pigment deposition  - Lesional cells were spindled, ovoid, and epithelioid, with open chromatin, prominent nucleoli, and without mitoses  - Mixed inflammatory infiltrate including neutrophils, histiocytes, and foamy macrophages  - Immunohistochemistry: Strongly positive for CD34; negative for S100, SOX10, HMB45, and Melan-A- Images:  Title: Figure 1 - Soft green-blue plaque on the dorsal hand  Title: Figure 2A - H&E stain demonstrating spindled cells surrounding fat globules  Title: Figure 2B - High-power H&E photomicrograph demonstrating pigmented and regular spindled cells surrounding fat globules  Title: Figure 2C - Lesional cells strongly positive for CD34

What is the most likely diagnosis?

reviewer_a.decisive_span: Strongly positive for CD34; negative for S100, SOX10, HMB45, and Melan-A
reviewer_a.reason: Dermatofibrosarcoma Protuberans (DFSP) is a distinct entity, typically characterized by diffuse CD34 positivity but also often by specific translocations (e.g., COL1A1-PDGFB) and a different histological appearance (storiform pattern, often with more cellularity and mitotic activity) than described here. The absence of mitoses and the specific mix of fibrous and adipose tissue with pigment deposition do not fit DFSP.

reviewer_b.decisive_span: negative for S100, SOX10, HMB45, and Melan-A
reviewer_b.missing_or_conflicting_component: DFSP typically shows CD34 positivity but lacks the prominent adipose and hemosiderin components; also usually has different histology.
reviewer_b.reason: DFSP is a different entity; the lesion's mixed fibrous-adipose and hemosiderotic features are not characteristic of DFSP.

clinical_record:
A male patient in his 20s presented with a 12-month history of asymptomatic red to brown macules and papules that initially appeared on his trunk and subsequently spread to the upper and proximal lower extremities. The lesions were symmetrically distributed and did not coalesce. His face, distal extremities, and mucous membranes were unaffected. The patient reported that some lesions had resolved spontaneously with residual hyperpigmentation. His medical history was unremarkable, and he did not take any medication on a regular basis.

- Multiple red to brown macules and papules on trunk and extremities- Symmetrically distributed lesions that did not coalesce- Face, distal extremities, and mucous membranes unaffected- No lymphadenopathy- Other systems review unremarkable

Laboratory Tests:- Blood cell count showed hypereosinophilia (4220/μL; reference range 50-250/μL)- Elevated tryptase (33.7 ng/mL; reference range <11.5 ng/mL)- Elevated vitamin B12 (>6000 pg/mL; reference range 211-911 pg/mL)- Negative serologic tests for HIV, hepatitis A, B, and C- Negative tests for parasitic infectionsImaging Studies:- CT of chest, abdomen, and pelvis: no pathologic findings- Cranial MRI: no pathologic findingsPathological Findings:- Skin biopsy (chest and upper extremity):  - Nodular infiltration of histiocytes with lymphocytes and eosinophils in upper dermis  - No lipid-laden foam cells or multinucleated giant cells  - Immunohistochemistry: CD68 positive, stabilin 1 positive, S-100 protein weakly positive, CD1a negativeBone Marrow Analysis:- Hypercellularity with myeloid hyperplasia- Increased eosinophils (20%, reference range <5%)- FIP1L1-PDGFRA fusion gene positive on RT-PCR

What is the most likely diagnosis?
reference_diagnosis: FIP1L1-PDGFRA–positive chronic eosinophilic leukemia (CEL) with associated generalized eruptive histiocytosis (GEH)

reviewer_a.decisive_span: hypereosinophilia (4220/μL; reference range 50-250/μL)
reviewer_a.missing_or_conflicting_component: specific etiology (FIP1L1-PDGFRA) and associated condition (generalized eruptive histiocytosis)
reviewer_a.reason: Hypereosinophilic syndrome is a broader category that includes chronic eosinophilic leukemia, but it lacks the specific genetic mutation and the associated histiocytosis mentioned in the reference.

reviewer_b.decisive_span: FIP1L1-PDGFRA fusion gene positive
reviewer_b.missing_or_conflicting_component: Missing the specific diagnosis of CEL and the associated GEH; HES is a broader category that includes CEL but does not specify the genetic cause.
reviewer_b.reason: Hypereosinophilic syndrome is a broader term; the record supports CEL with a specific fusion gene, so HES is a parent category rather than the exact diagnosis.

clinical_record:
A woman in her 40s presented with blurred vision in the right eye. She was undergoing treatment with systemic steroids, durvalumab (a PD-L1 inhibitor), and bevacizumab. Ten days after initial presentation, the patient developed sudden vision loss in the right eye.

Initial examination: Visual acuity of 20/25 OU. Right eye showed full visual field, right-sided relative afferent pupillary defect, unremarkable anterior segment, and mild swelling of the optic disc. Left eye had normal fundus and visual function. Follow-up examination (after vision loss): Right eye showed no light perception vision, marked swelling of the optic disc, peripapillary retinal hemorrhages, and occlusion of the superior branch artery. clinical_record:
A man in his 70s presented with swelling of the manubrium 12 years after resection of a large left substernal thyroid lobe through a midline sternotomy approach. The swelling was slightly tender and had increased in size markedly over the month prior to presentation. Medical history includes previous substernal left hemithyroidectomy for benign goiter 12 years ago.

Swelling noted over the manubrium, which was slightly tender.

- Imaging Studies:    CT Image Title: Computed Tomographic Image Demonstrating Lytic Mass of Manubrium    CT Image Description: Shows a lytic lesion replacing the manubrium measuring 2.7 × 4.4 × 5.8 cm and residual right goiter. The posterior aspect is in close proximity to the brachiocephalic artery and the left innominate vein.    - Fine-needle aspiration:    Revealed follicular thyroid cells in the goiter and the manubrial lesion.    - Pathological Examination:    Image Title: Thyroid Follicles With Nuclear Features Infiltrating Adjacent to Bone Trabeculae    Image Description: Hematoxylin-eosin stained specimens showing thyroid follicles infiltrating adjacent to bone trabeculae (at ×20 and ×10 magnification).

What is the most likely diagnosis?

reviewer_b.missing_or_conflicting_component: follicular subtype and manubrial invasion not specified

clinical_record:
A man in his early 60s with pathologic myopia had undergone multiple procedures, including vitrectomy and cataract surgery, on the left eye for a rhegmatogenous retinal detachment 2 years previously. He subsequently had received multiple intravitreous ranibizumab injections to the left eye for myopic choroidal neovascularization.

Best-corrected visual acuities were 20/40 OD and 20/200 OS.

- Multimodal imaging: Revealed emulsified silicone oil forming a meniscus in the fovea of the left eye.    - En face imaging with swept source optical coherence tomography: Demonstrated the confinement of the hyperoleon within a lamellar macular hole.    Image Titles and Descriptions:  1. Color images of the left fundus  2. Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (OCT) showing hyperreflective dots within a lamellar macular hole  3. En face swept source OCT showing oil bubbles within its boundaries

clinical_record:
A 42-year-old African American male presented with a 7-month history of fatigue, exertional dyspnea, arthralgias, hand swelling, tender ulcerations, hair loss, and a 50-pound weight loss. He had been hospitalized 6 months prior for hypoxia. He had been treated with prednisone previously.

clinical_record:
A 13-year-old boy presented with an intensely pruritic skin eruption that appeared approximately 24 hours after intensive sun exposure in spring. The patient was otherwise healthy but reported an episode of malaise and headache 2 weeks before first presentation. He had no history of photosensitivity, and denied the use of any topical or systemic photosensitizers.

Erythema and helical thickening as well as numerous small blisters, 2 to 3 mm in diameter, were present on both ears. Similar vesicles were observed at the upper and lower vermillion border. Several erythematous papules and crusts were located on the cheeks, neck, and lower arms.

- Laboratory tests: Differential blood count, routine chemical analysis, and serum porphyrins were unremarkable. Serum parvovirus B19 (PVB19) IgM and IgG antibodies were detectable. Bacterial cultures from blister fluid were unremarkable.- Virologic analyses: Negative results for herpes simplex viruses 1 and 2, varicella zoster virus, Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, human herpesvirus 6, hepatitis B and C viruses, 8 human polyomaviruses, and enteroviruses. PVB19 DNA was found (viral load of 0.2 PVB19 DNA copies/β-globin gene copy, or 33,438 copies/μg of isolated DNA) in lesional skin biopsy specimen, but not in the serum.- Other tests: Standard phototesting with UV-A and UV-B was unremarkable.- Images:  Image 1 Title: The Patient's Clinical Findings on the Ears at First Presentation  Image 1 Description: Helical thickening, erythema, and numerous small vesicles are present on both ears  Image 2 Title: The Patient's Facial Lesions  Image 2 Description: Crusted papules and small erosions are located on the cheeks. Several blisters are located at the upper and lower vermillion border

reviewer_a.reason: Erythema multiforme is a different condition with distinct clinical features and triggers, not supported by the provided clinical record.

A man in his 50s presented with pink-purple dermal papules and polyarticular inflammatory arthritis involving the wrists, metacarpophalangeal joints, and proximal interphalangeal joints. A woman in her 50s with stage IV B-RAF V600E mutant malignant melanoma with metastases of the liver, lungs, and peritoneum (primary site unknown). Within 2 weeks of starting ipilimumab treatment, she developed skin symptoms. After initial improvement and later disease recurrence, she received a second course of ipilimumab 14 months later, which led to recurrence and worsening of symptoms.

Physical findings included:- Photodistributed erythematous to violaceous eruption- Diffuse erythema of forehead and midface, involving nasolabial folds- Erythema and edema of upper eyelids- Diffuse erythema of upper chest and upper back- Flagellate erythema on posterior neck- Flat-topped pink to erythematous papules over knuckles- Prominent erythema at nailfolds with dilated capillary loops, capillary dropout, and ragged cuticles- Grade 4/5 strength on resisted abduction of shoulders bilaterally- Limited flexion of both hips- Reduced activity level due to weakness and early fatigue

Laboratory Tests:- Creatine kinase: 1088 U/L (increased to 1854 U/L)- Aldolase: 23.0 U/L- C-reactive protein: 28.6 mg/L- Antinuclear antibody titer: 1:640 with speckled pattern- Jo-1 antibody: negativeImaging Studies:- MRI showed mild short TI inversion recovery hyperintensity of bilateral vastus lateralis and rectus femoris musclesBiopsy Results:- Vastus lateralis muscle biopsy showed atrophy of type II muscle fibers without evidence of inflammatory myositis (note: performed after corticosteroid treatment)

clinical_record:
A 65-year-old woman presented with blurry vision in her right eye for several months. Ocular history included 3 recurrent episodes of bilateral iritis occurring during 5 months, amblyopia in the left eye, and bilateral posterior chamber intraocular lens. Patient had undergone left-sided mastectomy 2.5 years prior and had been on anastrozole therapy for more than 2 years. Medical history and past medication use were otherwise unremarkable.

Visual acuity: 20/25 OD and 20/150 OS without improvement on pinhole testing. Intraocular pressures were normal. Right eye showed trace conjunctival injection without definite ciliary flush, 2+ fine keratic precipitates, and 1+ cells in the anterior chamber. Left eye had a few keratic precipitates. Dilated fundus examination revealed cystoid macular edema with a yellow spot in the fovea in the right eye and an epiretinal membrane in the left eye. No inflammation in the periphery was noted in either eye.

- Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT):  Image Title: OCT Scans  Image Description: Right eye showed significant cystoid macular edema and subfoveal fluid. Normal findings for tick-borne and bacterial diseases.- Imaging:  Computed tomography of the chest was unremarkable.

A 29-year-old primigravida woman presented to the outpatient obstetric clinic for a routine antenatal checkup. There was no history of dyspnea, chest pain, palpitation, or lower limb swelling. Her vital parameters were within normal limits.

clinical_record:
A woman in her 80s with a history of nonischemic cardiomyopathy and chronic kidney disease presented with purpuric lesions on her face, elbows, knees, and feet. She was initially admitted for altered mental status in the setting of an unwitnessed fall and was noted to have 'bruises' on her lower extremities. New lesions developed on her nose, ear, and the extensor surfaces of her arms bilaterally.

The patient's nose, bilateral cheeks, forehead, and left ear (helical rim and antihelix) were found to have dusky purpuric macules and patches. Her knees, feet, and the extensor surfaces of her arms had reticulated purpuric macules and patches. There was skin sloughing off the lesions on her elbows and knees.

- Laboratory tests:     - Hypercalcemia (calcium level, 11.5 mg/dL)    - Acute kidney injury (creatinine level, 5.6 mg/dL)    - Rouleaux and cryoprotein precipitate on peripheral blood smear    - Abnormal paraprotein band on serum and urine protein electrophoreses    - Monoclonal IgG-κ protein on immunofixation electrophoresis    - Elevated serum cryoglobulin levels (cryocrit, 16%)    - Negative results for hepatitis, antinuclear antibodies, rheumatoid factor, heparin-induced thrombocytopenia antibodies, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies  - Biopsy findings:    Four-millimeter punch biopsy specimens from left ear, right arm, and forehead showed multifocal intravascular fibrinoid material consisting of a mix of cryoglobulins and fibrin thrombi with relatively little vessel wall inflammation  - Imaging studies:    CT scan of pelvis revealed lytic bony lesions      - Bone marrow biopsy:    Hypercellular marrow consisting of 80% plasma cells with atypical morphology and κ-light-chain restriction

What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 42-year-old patient with night blindness since childhood. The patient has been followed for 30 years, with initial presentation at age 10. The patient reports no symptoms except night blindness and is unaware of field loss. Past medical history is unremarkable.

clinical_record:
A man in his 20s presented to the emergency department with 1 day of chest pressure. Four days prior to presentation he experienced subjective fevers, rhinorrhea, a dry cough, and sinus congestion. The day prior to presentation he experienced 3 hours of substernal pressure that resolved spontaneously. In the early morning of the day of presentation, he was awakened from sleep by constant chest pressure radiating to the right jaw, diaphoresis, and 1 episode of vomiting. He reported no medical history.

Vital signs obtained in the Emergency Department were within normal limits. Cardiac examination revealed a regular rate and rhythm, normal point of maximum impulse without lifts, and no murmurs, rubs, or gallops in supine, sitting, or standing positions. The remainder of the physical examination was within normal limits.

- Laboratory Tests:
  * Initial serum troponin I level: 6.18 ng/mL
  * Elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein (values increased over next 3 days)

- Imaging and Other Tests:
  * ECG Findings: Normal sinus rhythm, ST-segment elevations with PR-segment depression in leads II, III, and aVF, ST-segment depression in lead V1, and PR-segment elevation in lead aVR
  * Coronary angiography: Normal coronary arteries, left ventricular end-diastolic pressure 12 mm Hg (reference range, 4-12 mm Hg)
  * Transthoracic echocardiogram: Normal results

What is the most likely diagnosis?

reviewer_a.reason: Acute Coronary Syndrome is ruled out by normal coronary angiography.

reviewer_b.missing_or_conflicting_component: Normal coronary arteries excludes acute coronary syndrome
reviewer_b.reason: ACS is ruled out by normal coronary angiography and the ECG pattern is not ischemic.

clinical_record:
A primigravid patient in their 20s during the eighth month of gestation presented with history of regular nonexertional episodic palpitations that lasted for a few minutes and subsided spontaneously over the past several days. The patient had no associated sweating, syncope, dyspnoea, orthopnoea, or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea. Visible neck pulsation was noticed by the patient's mother. The patient had no chronic medical comorbid conditions and was not taking any medications.

Blood pressure was 110/70 mm Hg and heart rate was 120 beats/min. The general examination was unremarkable. The jugular venous pulsations revealed regular cannon waves, and auscultation was significant for a variable first heart sound. Examination findings of other systems were normal.

Regular P waves evident marching onto QRS complexes at a rate of 100-125 beats/min with mean cycle length of 517.16 milliseconds with varying PR intervals.

clinical_record:
A 36-year-old man with end-stage renal disease secondary to IgA nephropathy underwent a live-related renal transplant 6 months ago and has been maintained on tacrolimus 3.5 mg daily, mycophenolate sodium 720 mg daily, and prednisolone 7.5 mg daily. He presented with a 14-day history of low-grade fever, dry cough, and anorexia without dyspnea, chest pain, hemoptysis, or weight loss. He was afebrile on admission, heart rate 88 beats/min, blood pressure 122/76 mm Hg, respiratory rate 28 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. Examination revealed bilateral inspiratory crackles; other findings were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 14.6 g/dL; total lymphocyte count 9900/μL; absolute neutrophil count 7720/μL; platelets 285 000/μL; serum creatinine 1.05 mg/dL. Arterial blood gas analysis demonstrated PaO₂ 68 mm Hg and an A–a gradient of 22 mm Hg. HIV ELISA was negative. Chest radiograph revealed bilateral diffuse alveolar infiltrates. High-resolution CT of the chest showed bilateral diffuse ground-glass opacities without pleural or mediastinal abnormalities.

Sputum induction was non-diagnostic. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid was positive for Pneumocystis jirovecii on Grocott’s methenamine silver stain and negative for acid-fast bacilli, CMV inclusion bodies, and fungal hyphae. He was treated with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and a prednisone taper, with clinical and radiographic resolution of infiltrates after 2 weeks.

Three weeks into therapy, he was asymptomatic except for an occasional dry cough. TMP-SMX was discontinued, and prednisolone was maintained at 10 mg daily. Laboratory studies then showed leukopenia (TLC 1400/μL; ANC 1050/μL). Chest radiograph revealed new left upper-zone infiltrates. Repeat HRCT showed resolution of ground-glass opacities and new patchy peribronchovascular consolidations in the right upper lobe, left upper lobe, and left lower-lobe apical segment. Repeat BAL was negative for AFB, fungus, and Pneumocystis jirovecii. 

Transbronchial lung biopsy from the left upper lobe showed alveoli filled with inflammatory debris consisting of granulation tissue, interstitial inflammation, and areas of intra-alveolar fibrin deposition.

reviewer_a.reason: The initial presentation was Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, but the candidate refers to the later, distinct diagnosis for which the BAL was negative for P. jirovecii.

reviewer_b.missing_or_conflicting_component: Initial infection, not the final diagnosis after resolution and new infiltrates
reviewer_b.reason: PJP was the initial diagnosis, but the reference is the subsequent organizing pneumonia; PJP is a related differential or prior manifestation, not the final object.

clinical_record:
A 9-year-old girl with a small muscular ventricular septal defect presented with chest pain and dyspnea one week after recovering from an upper respiratory infection and after minor anterior chest trauma in a fall. She was afebrile. Heart rate was 104 beats/min, respiratory rate 28 breaths/min, blood pressure 113/66 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation normal. Physical examination revealed mild tenderness over the sternum and normal cardiac auscultation. 

Chest radiography showed mild cardiomediastinal silhouette enlargement and a focal opacity in the right middle lung. ECG was normal. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a moderate circumferential pericardial effusion with right atrial collapse, normal biventricular systolic function, and no ventricular septal defect. 

Laboratory studies revealed a leukocyte count of 12,000 cells/µL with an absolute eosinophil count of 1,570 cells/µL (normal 40–190), C-reactive protein 1.94 mg/dL (normal <0.5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 45 mm/hr (normal 0–30), and troponin T 0.25 ng/mL (normal <0.1). Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging showed elevated global myocardial T2 (70 ms) and T1 (1150 ms) values, increased left ventricular wall thickness, a moderate pericardial effusion, and no late gadolinium enhancement.

She was admitted with a working diagnosis of viral myopericarditis. Treatment with oral ibuprofen and colchicine resulted in resolution of chest pain, normalization of troponin and inflammatory markers, and reduction of the pericardial effusion over three days. However, the absolute eosinophil count rose further. Consultations with infectious diseases, allergy/immunology, and rheumatology were obtained. Further history elicited pica and exposure to two dogs and a cat. 

Chest computed tomography revealed multiple pulmonary nodules with adjacent ground-glass opacities. An infectious workup showed negative PCR tests for influenza, respiratory syncytial virus, parainfluenza virus, rhinovirus, and adenovirus; negative Bartonella henselae titers; and a negative T-SPOT tuberculosis test. Mycoplasma pneumoniae IgM and IgG were elevated, but nasopharyngeal Mycoplasma PCR was negative. Toxocara serology was sent and was pending at discharge.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

reviewer_a.decisive_span: She was admitted with a working diagnosis of viral myopericarditis.
reviewer_a.reason: Viral myopericarditis was a working diagnosis that was not fully supported, especially given the persistent eosinophilia and negative viral PCRs. The patient's symptoms improved with anti-inflammatory treatment, but the underlying cause was not viral.

reviewer_b.decisive_span: working diagnosis of viral myopericarditis
reviewer_b.reason: Viral myopericarditis was the initial working diagnosis but is not the most likely final diagnosis given eosinophilia and exposure history.

A 25-year-old woman presented with a 1-month history of exertional dyspnea and palpitations. On examination, she had a systolic murmur. Bedside transthoracic ultrasound demonstrated moderate tricuspid regurgitation and possible pulmonary hypertension. A 20-month-old girl was evaluated for congenital soft-tissue masses and cutaneous vascular lesions. Since birth, she had multiple soft masses on the anterior upper chest, abdomen, and right arm. A large port-wine–colored capillary malformation partially involved her trunk. Examination of the extremities showed hypertrophy of the left thigh, overgrowth of both feet, and syndactyly of the second and third toes on the right. Dilated, tortuous veins were noted over the chest and left leg. She had no facial dysmorphism, no cardiac murmur, no organomegaly, full muscle strength, intact reflexes, and normal developmental milestones and growth parameters.

A 24-year-old man presented with a 1-year history of progressive left hip pain radiating to the anterior thigh. The pain began as a dull aching groin discomfort, worsened over weeks, was severe at night, and was associated with weight loss and anorexia. There was no history of trauma.

Rheumatologic evaluation, including serologic studies, was unremarkable. The initial clinical diagnosis was diffuse alveolar hemorrhage caused by SLE activity without sufficient clinical criteria of nosocomial pneumonia.

A 31-year-old woman presented with a 7-year history of episodic palpitations, profuse sweating, and severe headaches. Over the same period, she noted a gradually enlarging anterior neck swelling without compressive symptoms or signs of thyroid dysfunction. On examination, blood pressure was intermittently elevated during evaluation. A firm, non-tender anterior neck mass moved with deglutition; a second midline submental swelling was palpable at the level of the hyoid. 

Laboratory studies revealed:
- 24-hour urinary metanephrines >10 000 µg (normal 25–312 µg) and normetanephrines 8791 µg (normal <600 µg)

- CEA 2750 ng/mL (normal 0–5 ng/mL)  
- Intact PTH 128 pg/mL (normal 11.1–79.5 pg/mL)  
- Normal serum calcium, phosphorus, and vitamin D levels  
- Mild elevations in SGOT, SGPT, and ALP; other labs unremarkable  

A high-resolution neck ultrasound showed:
- Right thyroid lobe: 1.5 × 1.8 cm well-defined hypoechoic nodule with calcifications  
- Left thyroid lobe: 1.9 × 3 cm hypoechoic solid–cystic nodule with calcifications  
- Midline submental solid–cystic lesion with internal calcifications

clinical_record:
A 35-year-old man presented for routine follow‐up 11 years after a left total hip arthroplasty with a ceramic‐on‐ceramic articulation. Over the preceding 3 months, he had left buttock and greater trochanteric pain, initially attributed to overuse. He denied fevers or systemic symptoms. On examination, range of motion of the left hip was full and painless; there was focal tenderness over the posterior buttock and greater trochanter but no palpable mass. Anteroposterior radiographs of the pelvis and left hip were unchanged compared with images obtained 1 year earlier. A diagnosis of greater trochanteric bursitis was made, and an intra‐bursal corticosteroid injection was administered, resulting in partial symptom relief.

Six weeks later, he returned with persistent buttock pain and intermittent electric shock–like sensations radiating down the left leg. Physical examination now revealed decreased and painful range of motion of the left hip with continued tenderness over the greater trochanter. A lumbar spine radiograph was normal. Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 22 mm/h (reference range, 2–28), a C‐reactive protein level of 14.4 mg/L (reference, <10.0), and an alkaline phosphatase level of 318 IU/L (reference, 40–125). Hip aspiration yielded 10,750 white cells/μL; all cultures were negative. Serum cobalt and chromium levels were within normal limits. A metal artifact reduction sequence MRI revealed a left periprosthetic soft‐tissue mass measuring 9 × 8 × 10 cm, without bony involvement or bone‐marrow edema.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

reviewer_a.decisive_span: metal artifact reduction sequence MRI revealed a left periprosthetic soft‐tissue mass measuring 9 × 8 × 10 cm
reviewer_a.reason: Adverse Local Tissue Reaction (ALTR) is a plausible diagnosis given the periprosthetic mass and history of hip arthroplasty, but the reference diagnosis is osteosarcoma, which is a different entity.

reviewer_b.decisive_span: left periprosthetic soft-tissue mass measuring 9 × 8 × 10 cm
reviewer_b.reason: ALTR is a plausible related differential given the mass and arthroplasty, but the reference is osteosarcoma, a different entity. ALTR is not equivalent to osteosarcoma.

clinical_record:
A 15-year-old girl presented with multiple swellings of five months’ duration. She noted progressive enlargement of bilateral neck masses and one each on her back and anterior abdominal wall, without pain. There was no significant past medical, personal, or family history. 

On examination, there were seven subcutaneous, nontender, mobile swellings measuring 1×1 to 3×3 cm in the cervical regions, right paraspinal area, and anterior abdominal wall. The lesions were firm to hard without changes in the overlying skin. 

Complete blood count, metabolic panel, and skeletal survey were all normal. With a clinical impression of lymphoreticular malignancy or metastatic disease, fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) was performed on the most prominent swellings (two cervical, one paraspinal, one abdominal). 

Cytology smears from all sites showed moderate cellularity with similar features: predominantly plump spindle cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, fragments of collagenous matrix, and occasional small cells with scant cytoplasm. The spindle cells had bipolar cytoplasmic extensions and round-to-oval nuclei with fine granular chromatin; nucleoli were inconspicuous. Nuclear hyperchromasia, pleomorphism, or atypicality was not seen, and mitoses were sparse. There was no necrosis or inflammatory cells. 

Ultrasonography confirmed that all lesions were confined to the subcutaneous tissue, with no lymphadenopathy or deeper masses.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

reviewer_a.decisive_span: multiple swellings of five months’ duration
reviewer_a.reason: Nodular fasciitis typically presents as a solitary, rapidly growing lesion, which contradicts the multiple, slowly growing lesions described in the case.

reviewer_b.decisive_span: multiple swellings of five months’ duration
reviewer_b.missing_or_conflicting_component: Nodular fasciitis is typically solitary and self-limited, not multiple and progressive.
reviewer_b.reason: The clinical presentation of multiple subcutaneous nodules in a child is not typical for nodular fasciitis, which is usually a solitary, rapidly growing lesion.

A 35-year-old West African man with no prior psychiatric or medical history presented to clinic with a 1-week history of escalating behavioral changes. His family reported episodes of talkativeness, incoherent speech, visual and auditory hallucinations, insomnia, and grandiose and persecutory delusions. He denied head injury, substance use, or stressors and had no family history of psychiatric illness. He worked as a mechanical engineer in a mining community with potential mercury exposure and had no systemic or respiratory symptoms despite known community spread of COVID-19.

He appeared disheveled, restless, and agitated but was oriented to time, place, and person. Speech was loud and clear without latency. He exhibited circumstantial thought, grandiose delusions (“I am a prophet of God”), persecutory delusions, and both auditory (“gunshots”) and visual (a mob) hallucinations. Memory was intact and he had no insight.

Malaria and typhoid screens were negative. Urinalysis revealed transient proteinuria and glycosuria that normalized on repeat. Head CT scan was normal. A lateral flow COVID-19 antigen test and confirmatory RT-PCR were both positive.

clinical_record:
A 52-year-old woman was referred to endocrinology in 2011 for a 2-month history of right-sided neck swelling, worsening dysphagia, and mild pain. Her past medical history was notable for excision of a dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans in the left inguinal–suprapubic region in 1998, with four local recurrences (2000, 2001, 2008, and 2009) treated surgically; she also received external radiotherapy (66 Gy) after the last excision.

On examination, there was a large, firm, mildly tender mass on the right side of the neck without fixation; the Pemberton sign was positive. Laboratory studies showed:
• TSH 0.363 mIU/L (0.32–5.0)  
• Free T4 14.6 pmol/L (9.0–19.0)  
• Anti-thyroglobulin antibody 1 U/mL (< 1)  
• Anti-thyroid peroxidase antibody 1 U/mL (< 1)  
• Intact PTH 6 pmol/L (1.48–8.43)

Ultrasound of the thyroid revealed a right lobe volume of 50 mL and left lobe 7.3 mL; the entire right lobe was replaced by a hypo- to anechoic mass measuring approximately 6 × 4 × 6 cm, displacing the trachea 1 cm to the left, with no pathological lymphadenopathy. Fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the right lobe yielded a hemorrhagic background with isolated clusters of pleomorphic round and oval nuclei; it was classified as category IV/3, suspicious for primary or secondary malignancy.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck and thorax confirmed a voluminous right thyroid mass and detected two pulmonary nodules consistent with metastases. MRI showed no lymphadenopathy. Laryngoscopy demonstrated freely mobile vocal cords.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

reviewer_a.reason: There is no evidence in the record to suggest anaplastic thyroid cancer. The FNA was suspicious for primary or secondary malignancy, but not specifically anaplastic.

reviewer_b.decisive_span: Anaplastic thyroid cancer
reviewer_b.missing_or_conflicting_component: Anaplastic thyroid cancer is a primary thyroid malignancy, not a metastasis from DFSP
reviewer_b.reason: The candidate asserts a different disease entity (primary anaplastic thyroid carcinoma) that conflicts with the reference diagnosis of metastatic DFSP.

clinical_record:
A 56-year-old African American woman with no significant past medical history presented with a six-day history of progressive swelling of the left labia, which ruptured and began draining serosanguinous fluid two days before admission. On arrival, her temperature was 36.8 °C, blood pressure 100/60 mmHg despite intravenous fluid resuscitation, pulse 96‒100 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 17.4 × 10^9/L. Empiric intravenous vancomycin and piperacillin/tazobactam were initiated, and a surgical consultation was obtained. Pelvic CT imaging demonstrated an ulceration of the left labia with air in the subcutaneous fat of the left groin and lower abdominal wall, as well as inflammatory fat stranding along the left lateral abdominal wall. The Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotizing Fasciitis (LRINEC) score was calculated as 3, with the potential to rise to 7 pending C-reactive protein results. Despite non-definitive laboratory and imaging findings, concerns for sepsis, subcutaneous gas on CT, and the LRINEC score led to the decision to proceed with immediate exploratory surgery.

A 26-year-old woman presented with a 2-day history of burning on urination, urinary frequency, nocturia, and constant 5/10 suprapubic pain that did not radiate. She denied fever, nausea, vomiting, changes in bowel movements, weight change, palpitations, heat or cold intolerance, peripheral edema, and abnormal vaginal discharge. Her last menstrual period was one week earlier. Physical examination revealed lower abdominal tenderness, most pronounced in the para-umbilical area, without costovertebral angle tenderness.

Laboratory tests showed a negative serum β-hCG, normal CBC and BMP, and a urinalysis with 10–25 WBCs per high-power field, moderate bacteria, moderate mucus, moderate yeast, and positive nitrites; cervical NAAT was negative for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis. A diagnosis of lower urinary tract infection was made, and she received a 10-day course of antibiotics as an outpatient.

Despite treatment, her dysuria, frequency, and burning worsened. She reported chronic constipation, with two hard, non-bloody stools per week managed intermittently with stool softeners. There was no history of abdominal trauma or family gastrointestinal disease. 

Because of persistent symptoms, a contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis was performed. It demonstrated a 4.0 × 3.3 × 6.8 cm multiloculated, enhancing hypodense and isodense mass extending superiorly from the dome of the bladder to the posterior surface of the umbilicus, with surrounding acute inflammatory stranding and minimal fluid. There was possible invasion into the bladder dome, secondary thickening of an adjacent distal small-bowel loop, and perivesical stranding around a thick-walled, collapsed bladder.

Given these findings, differential diagnoses included patent urachus, urachal sinus, urachal diverticulum, and malignant transformation of a urachal remnant, and diagnostic laparoscopy was planned.

A 35-year-old man from rural north India presented with a one-month history of a progressively enlarging, central abdominal lump. Three weeks after the lump appeared, he developed intermittent high-grade fever and dull, aching abdominal pain. He had no significant past medical history. A 66-year-old white man presented to the Emergency Department with abrupt onset of dyspnea, palpitations, and lightheadedness. In the ED, he was found to be in monomorphic ventricular tachycardia and was electrically cardioverted into normal sinus rhythm. His medical history included a cerebrovascular accident, Factor V Leiden and prothrombin gene mutations, hypertension, incidentally noted pulmonary nodules, and chronic kidney disease (baseline GFR 40–45 mL/min/1.73 m2). He was taking losartan and warfarin and had no family history of sudden cardiac death.

Initial laboratory studies were within normal limits, and coronary angiography ruled out ischemia. His electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm without ischemic changes, but an epsilon wave in V1, a QRS duration of 140 ms, and T-wave inversions in leads V1–V5. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed preserved left ventricular function and no valvular disease, but a markedly dilated right ventricle with severely reduced systolic function. Based on an epsilon wave in V1–V3, T-wave inversions in V1–V3 with QRS >110 ms, an RV outflow tract dimension >32 mm, and severe RV dilation and hypokinesia, arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia was highly suspected. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging was indicated but not performed because of chronic kidney disease and patient preference. A septal endomyocardial biopsy was considered but deferred due to its low yield. Given the patient’s pulmonary nodules, cardiac sarcoidosis remained in the differential diagnosis.

A 32-year-old Caucasian woman presents with severe left knee pain and bilateral genu valgum deformity. She recalls being told she “may have had rickets” at age 9 but was lost to follow-up. At 22, she had trochanteric bursitis and an X-ray showed a Q-angle of 17°; no metabolic evaluation was done. She takes OTC vitamin D3 without calcium. She is 155 cm tall, weighs 58.5 kg (BMI 23.8), with no personal or family history of fractures or metabolic bone disease.

On exam, there is marked bilateral valgus alignment (left > right) with a knocking gait. Repeat X-ray shows a Q-angle of 23°. Bone density scanning reveals osteopenia of the left femoral head and normal lumbar spine density. Laboratory studies show:
• Serum phosphate: low  
• Total 25-hydroxyvitamin D and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D: elevated  
• Parathyroid hormone: low  
• FGF23: undetectable  

A 24-hour urine collection demonstrates inappropriately normal phosphate excretion for the degree of hypophosphatemia and normal urine calcium. Renal ultrasound reveals bilateral medullary nephrocalcinosis without stones.

A 25-year-old man with a history of Hodgkin lymphoma presented with a 2-month history of a gradually enlarging mass over the dorsum of his left hand. A male infant was delivered at 34 weeks’ gestation by cesarean section for fetal growth restriction and oligohydramnios. A 36-year-old woman presented with a 7-day history of right-sided chest pain and dyspnea without fever or cough. She reported two prior spontaneous pneumothoraces: one right-sided in 2018 managed medically, and one left-sided in 2019 treated surgically. She also noted occasional small-volume hemoptysis. 

On admission, she was alert, with SpO2 97% on room air. Right chest auscultation revealed hypoventilation; no crackles were appreciated. The remainder of the examination, including endocrine and genitourinary systems, was unremarkable. 

Laboratory studies (CBC, chemistry, urinalysis) were within normal limits; microbiological tests for tuberculosis and other bacteria were negative. 

Chest radiography showed lung hyperinflation without focal parenchymal abnormalities. HRCT of the chest revealed a small right pneumothorax and numerous round, thin-walled air cysts (2–5 mm) scattered in both lungs; no irregular cyst shapes were noted. 

Pulmonary function testing demonstrated a 6-minute walk distance of 67% predicted, normal DLCO, and a negative bronchodilator response. 

Thirteen days later, she developed left-sided chest pain and dyspnea. Chest X-ray confirmed a new left pneumothorax; CT again showed a large left pneumothorax with passive atelectasis and persistent small air cysts bilaterally. Thoracoscopic surgery with pleural drainage was performed, and lung biopsies were obtained. 

Three months later, she had bilateral pneumothoraces requiring a third thoracoscopic intervention. One month after discharge, repeat CT showed resolution of pneumothorax, persistent small air cysts, and faint nodular infiltrates in both lower lobes.
