clinical_record:
A 19-year-old man with hepatitis C and intravenous heroin use was transferred for evaluation of altered mental status. He was found minimally responsive and arrived febrile and intermittently responsive (Glasgow Coma Scale 10), requiring intubation for airway protection. On examination, he had left upper- and lower-limb weakness (strength 2/5 and 3/5) without meningeal signs. Vital signs were stable. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (white blood cell count rising from 10.0 to 14.6 × 10^3/µL). Urine toxicology was positive for benzodiazepines and opiates. 

Noncontrast head CT demonstrated a hypodense area in the right basal ganglia with mass effect but no hemorrhage. Brain MRI revealed T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the right basal ganglia and internal capsule with mild surrounding edema, scattered small foci of restricted diffusion, and subtle punctate blooming on susceptibility-weighted images; there was no enhancement after gadolinium. Transthoracic echocardiography showed no valvular vegetations.

Lumbar puncture yielded an opening pressure of 23 cm H₂O and slightly hazy cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) with 538 WBCs/mm³ (57% polymorphonuclear leukocytes), protein 81 mg/dL, and glucose 57 mg/dL (serum 121 mg/dL); Gram stain was negative. Initial CSF studies were negative for acid-fast bacilli, herpes simplex virus PCR, and fungi. Empirical IV ceftriaxone, vancomycin, and acyclovir were begun; his leukocytosis improved but fever persisted. 

On hospital day 5 he became more obtunded. Repeat lumbar puncture showed an opening pressure of 30 cm H₂O, 1762 WBCs/mm³ (60% polymorphonuclear leukocytes), protein 123 mg/dL, glucose 30 mg/dL (serum 105 mg/dL), and no red cells. Rickettsial studies, multiple viral cultures including John Cunningham virus PCR, quantiferon gold, and protozoal investigations were also negative. Repeat MRI demonstrated progression with new involvement of the left basal ganglia, increased diffusion restriction, development of necrosis, and new peripheral contrast enhancement. 

Because the etiology remained unclear and the patient was deteriorating, a brain biopsy was planned.

reviewer_a.reason: PML is caused by the John Cunningham virus (JCV). The record explicitly states that 'John Cunningham virus PCR' was negative, ruling out PML.

clinical_record:
An 18-year-old African male with no prior medical history presented first with a 2-day history of tonsillitis and a new macular rash on his chest that extended to his arms. Three days later he developed abdominal cramping and multiple episodes of non-bloody, watery diarrhea without nausea or vomiting, along with fevers and joint pains in his wrists, elbows, and knees. Initial outpatient care included oral chlorhexidine, lozenges, and symptomatic treatment.

He was then seen at a local health facility with high fever, tachycardia, and within 24 hours became confused with rising serum creatinine (from 200 to 400 μmol/L). He received ceftriaxone, paracetamol, loperamide, and one dose of IV methylprednisolone, but continued to deteriorate and was transferred to our hospital.

On arrival he was febrile (40°C), hypotensive (70/40 mmHg), tachycardic (130 bpm), tachypneic (50 breaths/min), and hypoxemic (SaO2 86% on room air). GCS was 14/15. Lung exam revealed bilaterally coarse crepitations; cardiovascular exam an audible S3 gallop; abdomen distended and tense with hypoactive bowel sounds; musculoskeletal exam was normal. He received fluid resuscitation, central line placement, and norepinephrine at 0.4 μg/kg/min.

Laboratory data showed: WBC 27.1×10^9/L; Hb 10.9 g/dL; platelets 281×10^9/L; procalcitonin 71.6 ng/mL; CRP 287 mg/L; creatinine 494 μmol/L; urea 26.7 mmol/L; Na 128 mmol/L; K 4.87 mmol/L; HCO3– 15.5 mmol/L; blood gas pH 7.33, PCO2 23 mmHg, PO2 122 mmHg, HCO3– 19.8 mmol/L. Liver tests showed AST 1461 U/L and ALT 812 U/L; hepatitis A, B, C, and HIV screens were negative. Urinalysis had 3+ protein and 4+ blood without RBCs; urine albumin:creatinine ratio was 52.3 mg/mmol. Cardiac markers were elevated (troponin 17 137 ng/mL; CK > 7800 U/L).

A negative ASOT made rheumatic fever unlikely. Chest X-ray showed pulmonary edema and cardiomegaly; echocardiogram revealed dilated cardiomyopathy with EF 30–35% and normal valves. Abdominal CT demonstrated a distended bowel with splenic and renal infarcts. HRCT confirmed cardiomegaly with bi-basal atelectasis. Initial differentials included bacterial septic shock, vasculitis (antiphospholipid syndrome or medium-sized vessel vasculitis), and multisystem inflammatory syndrome.

He required intubation and increasing norepinephrine (0.7 μg/kg/min), meropenem, vancomycin, urgent dialysis, and cooling measures. An autoimmune panel showed low C3 (0.51 g/L) and C4 (0.04 g/L), and he received a low-dose steroid pulse (250 mg IV daily). Autoantibodies returned with a positive beta2-glycoprotein IgA antiphospholipid antibody and negative ANA, anti–dsDNA, ENA, pANCA, and cANCA. SARS-CoV-2 PCR from tracheal aspirate and nasal swab was negative.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

reviewer_a.decisive_span: Autoantibodies returned with a positive beta2-glycoprotein IgA antiphospholipid antibody
reviewer_a.reason: While antiphospholipid antibodies were positive, the overall clinical picture with preceding tonsillitis, rash, fever, multi-organ involvement, and elevated inflammatory markers points more strongly to MIS. Antiphospholipid syndrome was also listed as a differential, not the final diagnosis.

reviewer_b.decisive_span: antiphospholipid syndrome
reviewer_b.missing_or_conflicting_component: positive beta2-glycoprotein IgA but no thrombotic events; other APS features absent
reviewer_b.reason: Antiphospholipid syndrome was considered as a differential, but the positive antibody alone without thrombosis or obstetric morbidity does not fulfill APS criteria; it is a related differential rather than the final diagnosis.

A 29-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of progressive neck pain radiating to his left hand. The pain was described as electrical in nature and was associated with numbness in the C8–T1 dermatomes. Over the preceding week, he noted weakness in fine movements and a weak grip of the left hand. His medical and surgical history was unremarkable.

On examination, there was marked atrophy of the hypothenar and interosseous muscles of the left hand. Motor testing of the left hand revealed muscle strength of 3/5.

Preoperative computed tomography of the cervical spine showed marked osteolysis and collapse of the T1 vertebra, with an extensive paravertebral soft tissue component. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated that the lesion was intermediate to low signal on T1-weighted images, intermediate on T2-weighted images, and showed heterogeneous enhancement after gadolinium administration. The lesion involved the anterior and posterior longitudinal ligaments but did not significantly compromise the thecal sac.

clinical_record:
A 32-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of slow but progressive swelling near her gluteal cleft. She denied fevers, chills, pain, drainage, bleeding, or rectal bleeding. On examination, there was a 4 × 4 cm area of swelling just left of the natal cleft at the level of the tip of the coccyx, with mild blanching erythema of the overlying skin but no fluctuance, purulence, or visible pilonidal pits. Given a high suspicion for abscess, percutaneous aspiration was performed in clinic but no fluid was obtained. The differential diagnosis at this time included inclusion cyst and soft-tissue tumor. The patient was scheduled for surgical excision. In the operating room, a 6-cm vertical incision was made over the lesion in the prone jack-knife position. A complex and septated 6 × 4 × 4 cm mass was excised from the subcutaneous tissue near the coccyx, with a rim of healthy tissue; the mass was adherent to subcutaneous fat but did not involve the coccyx or anal sphincter. The specimen was oriented with sutures and sent for permanent pathology, and the wound was closed primarily.

reviewer_b.reason: Epidermoid cyst is a type of inclusion cyst and is a reasonable differential for a subcutaneous mass, but it is not the reference ependymoma and is not confirmed by pathology.

clinical_record:
A 58-year-old woman presented to the rheumatology clinic with a 2-month history of fatigue, weakness, polyarthritis, and joint swelling. Nine months earlier, she had been diagnosed with idiopathic pulmonary hypertension after a 3-year history of progressive dyspnea (now NYHA class IV) and orthopnea, without cough or sputum, accompanied by low-grade fever and night sweats. Echocardiography at that time showed a pulmonary arterial systolic pressure (PASP) of 80 mm Hg, a left ventricular ejection fraction of 60%, mild mitral regurgitation, and moderate to severe tricuspid regurgitation. Chest CT revealed alveolar infiltrates in the posterior segment of the left basal lobe and multiple 6–8 mm peripheral lung nodules. Vital signs were normal, and pulmonary function testing was within normal limits.

Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 45 mm/h, an antinuclear antibody titer of 1:320, and an anti-centromere antibody level of 94.8 AU/ml. Tests for anti–Scl-70, hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis C virus, and rheumatoid arthritis were negative.

On examination, there was effusion of the right second, third, and fourth metacarpophalangeal joints; right second and third proximal interphalangeal joints; left second, third, and fourth metacarpophalangeal joints; and left fourth and fifth proximal interphalangeal joints. Raynaud’s phenomenon was elicited by cold‐water immersion of the hands. Chest auscultation revealed coarse crackles. Repeat echocardiography showed a PASP of 55 mm Hg after treatment, and ECG demonstrated sinus bradycardia with P pulmonale and biphasic P waves.

A 39-year-old Caucasian man was referred for evaluation of severe rod–cone retinal dystrophy. He had no history of parental consanguinity. Since childhood he noted high bilateral myopia and nyctalopia; he underwent uneventful bilateral cataract extraction with 13D monofocal intraocular lenses 3 years earlier. His medical history was notable for moderate intellectual disability, transient neutropenia in childhood that resolved spontaneously, microcephaly, truncal obesity, and joint hyperextensibility of the hands, feet, ankles, and knees. He had appropriate social behavior despite intellectual disability. On examination, his facial features included a thick head of hair, bushy eyebrows, a short upturned philtrum, a high nasal bridge with a beak-shaped nose, and an ogival palate. 

Best-corrected visual acuity was 2/10 in each eye. Slit-lamp examination and intraocular pressure were normal. Fundus examination showed bilateral disc pallor, generalized arteriolar narrowing, mid-peripheral “bone-spicule” pigmentary changes, and retinal pigment epithelium atrophy. Macular optical coherence tomography demonstrated diffuse RPE and outer retinal atrophy involving the subfoveal region without cystoid macular edema. Peripapillary OCT revealed chorioretinal thinning with decreased retinal nerve fiber layer thickness (global RNFL thickness of 53 μm in the right eye and 75 μm in the left eye). Fluorescein angiography showed diffuse RPE atrophy with prominent choroidal vessels and mid-peripheral bone-spicule pigment mobilization. Full-field electroretinography demonstrated absent a- and b-waves in both dark- and light-adapted phases, and pattern ERG lacked a P50 wave. Axial lengths were 26.07 mm (right eye) and 26.13 mm (left eye). 

Thus, the patient presented with a syndromic pigmentary retinal dystrophy characterized electrophysiologically as rod–cone dysfunction with macular involvement, in the setting of high bilateral myopia, presenile cataracts, facial dysmorphism, transient childhood neutropenia, intellectual disability, truncal obesity, joint hyperextensibility, and microcephaly.

reviewer_a.missing_or_conflicting_component: polydactyly, renal anomalies, hypogonadism, learning disabilities (not intellectual disability)
reviewer_a.reason: While Bardet-Biedl syndrome also presents with rod-cone dystrophy, obesity, and intellectual disability, it typically includes polydactyly, renal anomalies, and hypogonadism, which are absent in this patient. The presence of transient neutropenia, microcephaly, joint hyperextensibility, and specific facial dysmorphism points away from Bardet-Biedl syndrome and towards Cohen syndrome.

reviewer_b.missing_or_conflicting_component: Bardet-Biedl syndrome typically includes polydactyly, renal anomalies, and hypogonadism, which are absent; the facial and hematologic features are more specific to Cohen syndrome.

A 53-year-old Hispanic man presented with painful left lower-extremity swelling and erythema. Six months earlier, incidentally noted bilateral adrenal and periaortic retroperitoneal masses were not further evaluated. He reported intermittent fevers, episodic night sweats, decreased appetite, and palpitations. He denied trauma or injury to the leg. On examination, the left calf had ill-defined, warm, confluent erythema, edema, and tender induration. Laboratory studies showed mild lymphocytopenia, moderate anemia, elevated creatine kinase, elevated aldolase, and elevated lactate dehydrogenase; peripheral-blood flow cytometry was unremarkable. CT and MRI of the leg revealed gastrocnemius myositis, extensive subcutaneous and superficial myofascial edema, and popliteal lymphadenopathy without evident lymphatic obstruction. He was started on intravenous ceftriaxone for presumed cellulitis and pyomyositis but did not improve. A punch biopsy of skin from the lower leg showed a sparse perivascular and interstitial infiltrate of enlarged atypical mononuclear cells in the reticular dermis and subcutis, not consistent with cellulitis.

A 46-year-old woman presented with right flank pain, dysuria, and hematuria. Her past medical history was notable for an abdominal hysterectomy 15 years earlier. General and pelvic examinations were unremarkable. Urinalysis showed 6–8 red blood cells and 4–6 pus cells per high-power field but no other abnormalities.

An ultrasound of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a focal hypoechoic polypoidal lesion measuring 3.4 × 2.8 cm along the anterosuperior wall of the urinary bladder, containing tiny hyperechoic foci; the outline of the adjacent bladder wall appeared indistinct. The uterus was not visualized; a cystic area was noted in the left adnexa, and both ovaries were not seen.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed a well-defined soft-tissue–density lesion with calcific specks along the anterosuperior bladder wall that demonstrated heterogeneous enhancement in the early arterial and venous phases. The intraluminal component merged with the bladder wall, causing minimal localized wall thickening; the rest of the bladder wall was normal. Additional findings included a right calyceal calculus with mild pelvicalyceal dilatation, a simple right renal cyst, no pelvic lymphadenopathy, and left hydrosalpinx.

On imaging, possibilities such as endometriosis, a mucosal neoplastic lesion, or a granulomatous lesion of the urinary bladder were considered.

clinical_record:
An 82-year-old man with epithelioid pleural mesothelioma (cT1N0M0) was treated with ipilimumab and nivolumab. After eight courses, follow-up chest CT showed new bilateral infiltrative shadows. He reported fever and dyspnea. Laboratory tests revealed elevated C-reactive protein and surfactant protein D levels; Krebs von den Lungen-6 was normal. Sputum cultures, procalcitonin, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR were negative. Serologic testing for anti–nuclear antigen, anti–aminoacyl–tRNA synthetase, anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide, anti-Sjögren’s-syndrome-related antigen A and B, and anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antigen antibodies were all negative. He had no history of antigen exposure. Immunotherapy was discontinued. He received lascufloxacin and then tazobactam/ceftolozane without improvement; oxygen requirement increased to 2 L/min. Based on the clinical picture and imaging, grade 3 ICI-induced pneumonitis was suspected. He underwent methylprednisolone 1000 mg/day for 3 days followed by prednisolone 60 mg/day for 8 days, but chest radiographs remained unchanged and oxygen needs rose to 4 L/min. A second course of methylprednisolone 1000 mg/day for 3 days produced no clinical improvement. One week later, bronchoscopy showed no airway secretions. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid contained 29% neutrophils, 58% lymphocytes, 13% macrophages, and a CD4/CD8 ratio of 0.33. Transbronchial lung biopsy showed no malignancy, and cultures of bronchoscopy specimens were negative. Based on these findings, he was diagnosed with steroid-refractory ICI-induced pneumonitis.

reviewer_a.reason: Ipilimumab-induced pneumonitis is a type of immune-related pneumonitis. However, the patient also received nivolumab, and the diagnosis was ICI-induced pneumonitis, not specifically ipilimumab-induced. The record also specifies steroid-refractory.

reviewer_b.missing_or_conflicting_component: nivolumab also implicated
reviewer_b.reason: Identifies one of the two checkpoint inhibitors as cause, but incomplete etiology.

clinical_record:
A 76-year-old woman with a history of appendicitis, torsion of an ovarian cyst pedicle, and uterine myoma presented with a rapidly enlarging right parietal mass behind the ear over one month. She had no neurological deficits or systemic symptoms. Laboratory studies, including complete blood counts, metabolic panel, and viral serology for HIV and Epstein-Barr virus, were all normal or negative. Noncontrast CT of the head revealed a 5-cm hyperdense meningeal mass with parietal bone invasion. Gadolinium-enhanced MRI showed a heterogeneously enhancing lesion in the right parietal region. Cerebral angiography demonstrated a vascular tumor supplied by the middle meningeal artery. Thus, a clinical diagnosis of osteoblastic meningioma was made, and the differential diagnosis included primary lymphoma, metastasis, and sarcoma. The patient underwent endovascular embolization of the feeding artery followed by surgical resection. Intraoperatively, the tumor was extradural, caused skull destruction, and had no intradural involvement. Histology showed a malignant spindle cell neoplasm with positive immunostaining for α-smooth muscle actin, vimentin, and desmin, and negative staining for Epstein-Barr virus.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

reviewer_a.reason: Hemangiopericytoma has a different immunohistochemical profile (typically CD34 positive, SMA negative) than what is described in the record.

reviewer_b.decisive_span: positive immunostaining for α-smooth muscle actin, vimentin, and desmin
reviewer_b.missing_or_conflicting_component: Hemangiopericytoma would not show smooth muscle actin and desmin positivity
reviewer_b.reason: Hemangiopericytoma is a different mesenchymal tumor with different immunophenotype; the provided histology supports leiomyosarcoma.

A 75-year-old Caucasian woman was admitted with a prosthetic hip infection 10 days after revision surgery. Her medical history included chronic kidney disease (baseline creatinine 130–150 μmol/L), hypertension, type 2 diabetes, heart failure, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and folate deficiency. Home medications included aspirin, bisoprolol, atorvastatin, furosemide, gliclazide, pantoprazole, folic acid, inhaled bronchodilators, and as-needed oxycodone. On admission she began intravenous vancomycin and acetaminophen for pain.

On hospital day 10 she developed drowsiness, confusion, disorientation, and hyperventilation. Examination showed a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 12. Temperature was 36.2°C, blood pressure 145/66 mmHg, pulse 80/min, respiratory rate 24/min, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Cardiopulmonary and neurologic examinations were otherwise unremarkable.

- Sodium 142 mmol/L, potassium 3.5 mmol/L, chloride 118 mmol/L, bicarbonate 5 mmol/L  
- Blood urea nitrogen 8 mmol/L, creatinine 150 μmol/L (baseline)

- Albumin 17 g/L  
Arterial blood gas: pH 7.18, pCO2 1.7 kPa, pO2 16.7 kPa, bicarbonate 8.3 mmol/L, base excess –22.7 mmol/L. The corrected anion gap was 25 mmol/L.

A 35-year-old woman presented with left fronto-orbital swelling of 10 years’ duration. She reported progressive deterioration of vision in her left eye over 1.5 years, to the point where she could barely perceive hand movements near her face. The proptosis had become more pronounced over the past month, and the left globe was displaced inferiorly and medially. There was no history of endocrine abnormalities.

A 16-year-old male with no prior medical history noted a small lump in his right hemiscrotum two months earlier during self-examination. clinical_record:
An 8‐year‐old boy with no significant past medical history presented with a 30-minute history of generalized abdominal pain followed by a single episode of vomiting. During the event he developed diaphoresis, mucocutaneous paleness, dizziness, dysarthria, incoherent speech, and lack of eye contact, without loss of consciousness, abnormal movements, or sphincter relaxation. The episode lasted 10 minutes, after which he reported a frontal headache (5/10) and persistent nausea. Family denied toxin or medication exposure. He had a similar episode 18 months earlier, diagnosed as migraine. There was no personal or family history of epilepsy or neurological disorders. Developmental milestones were age‐appropriate, and he was performing well in school.

On admission, his vital signs were normal except for blood pressure above the 95th percentile for age. Neurologic examination revealed confusion and disorientation; he could not recognize his mother or speak but could follow visual commands. Motor and sensory examinations were normal. Approximately 20 minutes after arrival, his consciousness and orientation improved. Over the next hours he had three additional self‐limited vomiting episodes and ongoing headache, which improved after a single IV dose of diclofenac (1 mg/kg).

Complete blood count, serum chemistries, and electrolytes (including sodium, chloride, potassium, magnesium, and phosphorus) were all within normal limits. Brain MRI with an epilepsy protocol was reported as normal for age.

clinical_record:
A 25-year-old nulliparous woman presented with a 1-month history of insidious-onset right lower abdominal pain. She also had lifelong non-pitting edema of the left leg extending to the labia majora. She was otherwise healthy, with regular menses and no tobacco or alcohol use. On examination, she was afebrile, blood pressure was 110/80 mmHg, pulse 88 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Cardiac and respiratory examinations were unremarkable. Neurologic exam was normal. Abdomen revealed a firm, non-tender, mobile mass measuring approximately 12 cm × 10 cm in the right lower quadrant; bimanual pelvic examination confirmed a right adnexal mass.  

Baseline hematologic, biochemical, thyroid, renal, and HIV/HBV/HCV serologies were within normal limits. Tumor markers were all in the reference range: carcinoembryonic antigen 1.14 ng/mL, lactate dehydrogenase 251 U/L, α-fetoprotein 2.16 ng/mL, CA-125 21 U/mL, and β-hCG 2.39 µIU/mL. Pap smear was negative.  

Transvaginal ultrasound showed multiple uterine fibroids and a large hypoechoic lesion in the right adnexa. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a well-marginated thin-walled solid-cystic lesion measuring 16.1 × 7.9 × 8.1 cm in the abdominopelvic region containing a 2.3 × 2.1 cm cystic component and a 5.8 × 5.7 cm solid component. A separate 7 × 3.2 × 2.8 cm cystic lesion was noted in the right parauterine region. Bilateral ovaries were not visualized separately. The uterus was bulky with multiple fibroids. Multiple small mesenteric lymph nodes were seen. Incidentally, a double inferior vena cava was identified, with the left cava draining via the left renal vein to the right-sided cava. Serology for filarial infection was negative.  

Although tumor markers were normal, the imaging findings were concerning for an ovarian neoplasm. A staging laparotomy with surgical excision was planned, with a provisional diagnosis of a malignant ovarian tumor in the setting of uterine fibroids and unilateral lymphedema.

clinical_record:
An 8-year-old girl was evaluated for recurrent seizures, left-sided weakness, and developmental delays. Seizures began at age 3 months, initially infrequent but progressively more frequent despite antiepileptic therapy. The parents also noted delayed motor and cognitive milestones and gradual behavioral changes, including disturbed sleep, irritability, and episodes of aimless talking. There was no family history of neurological disorders and no reported perinatal complications or trauma. 

On neurologic examination, she had significant cognitive impairment and marked left hemiparesis with brisk reflexes, consistent with an upper motor neuron pattern. Sensory examination and cranial nerves were unremarkable. Routine laboratory studies, including metabolic and infectious panels, were normal. Electroencephalography showed focal abnormal brain activity concordant with her seizure semiology. 

Brain magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated marked asymmetry of the cerebral hemispheres, with significant atrophy of the right cerebral hemisphere and ex vacuo dilatation of the right lateral ventricle. Ipsilateral calvarial thickening and compensatory hyperpneumatization of the right sphenoid bone and bilateral mastoid air cells were evident. In the right fronto-parieto-temporal region, there were areas of cystic encephalomalacia surrounded by gliosis, suggesting a remote focal brain injury.

reviewer_a.reason: Hemimegalencephaly is characterized by an enlarged cerebral hemisphere, whereas the patient's imaging shows significant atrophy of one cerebral hemisphere.

reviewer_b.decisive_span: atrophy of the right cerebral hemisphere
reviewer_b.missing_or_conflicting_component: Hemimegalencephaly implies enlargement, not atrophy; the record shows atrophy and encephalomalacia.
reviewer_b.reason: Hemimegalencephaly is a different malformation with hemispheric overgrowth, whereas the case shows atrophy and gliosis, incompatible with that diagnosis.

A 33-year-old man with no significant past medical history presented with a 3-month history of progressively worsening occipital headache, exacerbated by Valsalva maneuvers. On neurologic examination, he had bilateral past-pointing and an intention tremor. Brain MRI revealed a 6.9 × 5.5 × 6.1 cm lobulated mass centered at the left cerebellopontine angle, extending craniocaudally from the left ambient cistern to the premedullary space. The lesion involved and expanded Meckel’s cave, with a small extension into the left infratemporal fossa via the foramen ovale. It contained multiloculated T1-hypointense, T2-FLAIR–partially suppressible nonenhancing cystic areas with interspersed enhancing septa, as well as T1/T2-isointense enhancing solid components. Susceptibility-weighted imaging demonstrated curvilinear signal loss with corresponding T1 hyperintensity consistent with hemorrhagic foci, and diffusion-weighted imaging showed no diffusion restriction. There was compression of the left cerebellum and brainstem, dilation of the third, fourth, and lateral ventricles, anterior displacement of the cavernous sinus, and encasement with mild narrowing of the left petrous internal carotid artery; the masticator muscles were preserved. Noncontrast CT of the head showed smooth remodeling and erosion of the left petrous apex, clivus, carotid canal, and foramen ovale, along with two punctate calcifications; the internal auditory canals and inner ear structures were unremarkable.

reviewer_a.missing_or_conflicting_component: location (Meckel's cave vs. internal auditory canal)
reviewer_a.reason: Acoustic neuromas (vestibular schwannomas) arise from the vestibulocochlear nerve, typically in the internal auditory canal, not Meckel's cave.

reviewer_b.decisive_span: internal auditory canals and inner ear structures were unremarkable

reviewer_b.reason: The lesion does not involve the internal auditory canal, making acoustic neuroma unlikely.

A 28-year-old man was admitted with a 2-day history of intermittent, sharp, central chest pain with diaphoresis. The pain was pleuritic and worsened when he sat forward. He denied recent viral symptoms and had not received a COVID-19 booster. His medical history was significant for ulcerative colitis diagnosed 3 weeks earlier, for which he started mesalazine; his bowel symptoms had improved. He took no other medications and had no allergies. He smoked 3–4 cigarettes daily and denied alcohol or drug use. There was no family history of cardiovascular disease.

On examination he was hemodynamically stable; the only abnormal finding was stage 2 finger clubbing. ECG showed sinus rhythm with benign early repolarization in the anterior leads. Chest radiography was unremarkable. Laboratory tests revealed a hemoglobin concentration of 132 g/L (120–170), a low mean corpuscular volume of 75 fL (80–97), and a high-sensitivity troponin T of 275 ng/L (<14) peaking at 632 ng/L on hospital day 2. C-reactive protein was 59 mg/L (<5) rising to 173 mg/L. Serum viral and autoantibody screens were negative.

Transthoracic echocardiography showed a normal left ventricular size, borderline low systolic function (LVEF 50–55%) with dyssynchronous septal motion, and a normal right ventricle without pericardial effusion. Given his atypical pain, young age, and troponin rise, an invasive coronary angiogram was considered but deferred in favor of cardiac magnetic resonance imaging.

On hospital day 3, CMR demonstrated a normal-sized left ventricle with mild systolic dysfunction (LVEF 59%) and hypokinesia of the anterolateral and inferolateral segments. The basal lateral wall was thickened to 14 mm. The right ventricle was small with normal function. There was extensive patchy late gadolinium enhancement in a mid-wall to epicardial distribution, particularly in the basal and mid lateral wall. T2-weighted imaging suggested myocardial edema despite suboptimal image quality. There was no pericardial enhancement or effusion. These findings were consistent with an extensive inflammatory myocardial process.

reviewer_a.reason: This candidate identifies myocarditis, which is correct, but it lacks the specific etiology (mesalazine-induced) that is supported by the clinical record.

reviewer_b.decisive_span: extensive inflammatory myocardial process
reviewer_b.missing_or_conflicting_component: missing_etiology
reviewer_b.reason: Myocarditis is the correct disease family but lacks the specific mesalazine-induced etiology.

A 52-year-old man presented with a progressively enlarging, mildly tender right-flank subcutaneous nodule noted over two years. He had a history of HBV-positive hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) treated with partial hepatectomy, entecavir, transarterial chemoembolization, sorafenib, regorafenib, and pembrolizumab over the preceding two years. On admission, vital signs were: temperature 37.2°C, pulse 112/min, respiratory rate 19/min, blood pressure 114/78 mmHg. He denied alcohol or tobacco use.

Physical examination revealed an ~8×4 cm subcutaneous mass over the right hypochondriac and flank regions; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed: white blood cell count 8.93×10^3/µl, hemoglobin 13.8 g/dl, AST 55.7 U/l, ALT 55.7 U/l, lactate dehydrogenase 201 U/l, alpha-fetoprotein 157 ng/ml, CEA 7.99 ng/ml, CA19-9 21.6 U/ml, HBsAg reactive, HCV-PCR negative. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules. Abdominal CT showed multiple nodules in liver segments 5 and 7 (largest 3.5 cm) and a right-flank soft tissue mass invading the 12th rib measuring 8×4×4 cm. Based on the clinical history and imaging, extrahepatic metastasis of HCC was suspected, but a primary soft tissue sarcoma could not be excluded. After discussion, surgical excision of the flank mass was performed without complications.

A 41-year-old previously healthy man presented with a 2-year history of progressively worsening fever, weight loss, night sweats, and a dry cough. He also reported chronic lower back pain without neurologic deficits and a painful nonhealing ulcer on his right hallux. He had two sputum GeneXpert tests at local clinics, both negative. He was treated symptomatically with paracetamol, NSAIDs, and topical antibacterials.  

On referral for the toe ulcer, examination revealed a cachectic man who was normotensive and afebrile, with no lymphadenopathy or edema. He had tenderness over the thoracic spine but no neurologic deficits. Laboratory tests showed:  
• Hemoglobin 10.9 g/dL, white cells 7.3×10^9/L, platelets 369×10^9/L  
• ESR >130 mm/hr, CRP 113 mg/L  
• IgA 6.2 g/L, anti-DNase B 259 IU/mL  
• Negative ANA, anti-dsDNA, ANCA, HIV, hepatitis B and C, and syphilis serologies  
• Urine protein-creatinine ratio 0.242 g/mmol; dipstick: 3+ leukocytes, 3+ red blood cells; microscopy: granular casts; urine culture: no growth  

Chest radiograph showed bilateral reticular-nodular opacities. An induced sputum was trace positive for MTB on GeneXpert and subsequently grew MTB sensitive to rifampicin and isoniazid. A 58‐year‐old man presented to the emergency department with a 24‐hour history of right iliac fossa pain, nausea, and diarrhea. His surgical history was notable for a laparoscopic appendectomy performed 8 months earlier; he had no other significant past medical history. A 40-year-old previously healthy man was admitted after 1 week of progressive apathy, unresponsiveness, and immobility. He became bedridden and required a feeding tube and urinary catheter. On transfer, he was in a vegetative state.  
Vital signs: temperature 36.5 °C, heart rate 80 bpm, blood pressure 135/78 mmHg, Glasgow Coma Scale 7 (E3 V1 M3). Pupils 3.5 mm, briskly reactive; corneal reflexes present. Both axial and appendicular muscles were rigid, with flexed arms and extended legs; bilateral Babinski and Chaddock signs were positive.  
Laboratory studies: WBC 3.79×10^9/L, neutrophils 74%, CRP 6.07 mg/L, ESR 21 mm/h; HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B and C serologies negative; ANA, anticardiolipin, ANCA, and T-spot negative. Liver and renal functions were normal.  
Lumbar puncture: opening pressure 50 mmH₂O; CSF clear, protein 3.64 g/L, glucose 2.6 mmol/L (blood glucose 5.38 mmol/L), chloride 123 mmol/L, leukocytes 0/mm³. CSF India ink stain and bacterial cultures were negative. CSF oligoclonal bands, AQP4, MOG, and GFAP antibodies were negative; CSF fungal cultures were negative.  
Imaging: Brain CT showed a hypodense lesion in the corpus callosum. MRI revealed a homogeneous mass in the corpus callosum body, hypointense on T1, isointense on T2 FLAIR, with rim enhancement and surrounding vasogenic edema on postcontrast T1. DWI demonstrated rim hyperintensity but no central restricted diffusion.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

reviewer_a.reason: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease is a prion disease characterized by rapidly progressive dementia, myoclonus, and specific EEG/MRI findings (e.g., cortical ribboning, basal ganglia hyperintensity on DWI/FLAIR). The patient's presentation of progressive apathy, unresponsiveness, and immobility, along with a focal brain lesion and CSF findings, does not align with CJD.

reviewer_b.decisive_span: MRI revealed a homogeneous mass in the corpus callosum body
reviewer_b.reason: CJD typically presents with rapidly progressive dementia and characteristic MRI changes (cortical ribboning, basal ganglia hyperintensity) without a mass lesion. The presence of a rim-enhancing corpus callosum mass is not consistent with CJD.

A 20-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of intermittent abdominal pain, recurrent vomiting, and melena. She had no significant past medical history and no family history of cancer. On examination, she had mild abdominal tenderness; gynecological examination was normal. Laboratory studies revealed iron-deficiency anemia; white blood cell and platelet counts were normal. Upper and lower endoscopies were unremarkable. Magnetic resonance enterography demonstrated a focal segment of small-bowel wall thickening measuring 15 mm by 2 mm. An exploratory laparotomy revealed an exophytic ileal mass with mesenteric lymphadenopathy but no peritoneal or hepatic metastases. A wide segmental resection was performed without complication.

Gross examination showed a 30 mm by 25 mm polypoid, tan-white, lobulated mass arising from the small-intestinal wall. Microscopically, the lesion was a transmural, infiltrative proliferation of uniform epithelioid and spindle cells arranged in nested and fascicular patterns, with variable eosinophilic or clear cytoplasm, round to oval vesicular nuclei, inconspicuous nucleoli, and up to 10 mitoses per 10 high-power fields; there was mucosal ulceration but no melanin pigment, lymphovascular invasion, or perineural invasion, and three mesenteric lymph nodes were negative for tumor.

Immunohistochemical analysis showed diffuse, strong positivity for S100 protein and SOX10; HMB45 and Melan A were negative. There was patchy synaptophysin expression. CD117, DOG1, cytokeratin, CD34, smooth muscle actin, desmin, chromogranin, and CD56 were all negative.

A 68-year-old man with pseudophakic bullous keratopathy underwent Descemet Stripping Automated Endothelial Keratoplasty (DSAEK) in the right eye. His postoperative course was initially uneventful under topical and systemic corticosteroids. He had a history of an eye infection by Thaumetopoea pityocampa (pine processionary) 9 months before DSAEK, which had resolved prior to surgery.

Two months after DSAEK, he was referred for evaluation of keratitis in the right eye. On examination:
• Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/200 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye.  
• Pupils were isocoric and isoreactive without an afferent pupillary defect.  
• There was no pain with ocular movements.  
• Slit-lamp biomicroscopy of the right eye showed brown, multilobular lesions confined to the deep corneal stroma, with no conjunctival hyperemia, no discharge, and no epithelial defect.  
• The anterior chamber was deep and clear. Intraocular pressure and fundus examination were normal. The left eye was unremarkable.

A 64-year-old white man was admitted in March 2016 with acute-onset abdominal pain and anemia. He had been on therapeutic anticoagulation for paroxysmal “pre-shimmering.” His history included two hypervascular liver lesions in segment IV, first noted in August 2015; biopsies at that time showed histologically proven adenoma without malignancy. On presentation, he was hemodynamically stable but had a hemoglobin level of 4.4 mmol/L. He reported no weight loss, fever, or constitutional symptoms. Laboratory studies showed α-fetoprotein, carcinoembryonic antigen, and carbohydrate antigen 19-9 levels within normal ranges; serum human chorionic gonadotropin was not measured. Abdominal ultrasound revealed subcapsular hepatic bleeding. Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed active bleeding from one of the two hypervascular lesions in segment IV. After angiographic embolization and conservative management, bleeding resolved. In April 2016, follow-up CT showed persistent hypervascular lesions without typical features of hepatocellular carcinoma. Additional MRI demonstrated hypervascular lesions with central necrosis. Because of suspicion for an atypical hepatocellular carcinoma, an elective surgical resection was planned.

reviewer_a.reason: The record states 'suspicion for an atypical hepatocellular carcinoma' but does not confirm it as the final diagnosis. The initial biopsy showed adenoma.

reviewer_b.missing_or_conflicting_component: conflicts with biopsy-proven adenoma
reviewer_b.reason: HCC is a different malignancy not supported by biopsy; reference is choriocarcinoma, so also not equivalent.

An 18-month-old girl was brought for evaluation of a swelling in her left medial thigh. Over the past six months, the mass had enlarged gradually and was painless, with no history of trauma or infection. On examination, there was a firm, nonpulsatile mass measuring approximately 10 cm, fixed to underlying tissues but mobile relative to the overlying skin. There were no signs of inflammation, neurovascular impairment, or inguinal lymphadenopathy.

Laboratory tests were unremarkable. A CT scan of the thigh showed a well-defined, lobulated, hypodense mass in the left anteromedial compartment of the proximal thigh, extending toward the inguinal area. The lesion exhibited internal septations and a density similar to subcutaneous fat, displacing the common and superficial femoral vessels anterolaterally without signs of invasion; it abutted the proximal femoral bone but did not erode it.

An MRI confirmed a fatty-appearing, well-circumscribed mass with internal septations and no encasement of neurovascular structures.

A 61-year-old man presented with gross hematuria and intermittent right pelvic pain. His medical history included hypertension, psoriasis, treated pulmonary tuberculosis, and a 60–pack-year smoking history. Urinalysis revealed microscopic hematuria; biochemical tests were normal. A 14-year-old girl presented with 6 months of discomfort at the tip of the left middle finger. She had noted that the finger was larger than the others since birth and that it grew progressively. clinical_record:
A 74-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, ischemic stroke, peripheral arterial disease, bilateral nonobstructive renal artery stenosis, chronic right internal carotid occlusion, seizures, and vascular dementia was transferred from a nursing home because of decreased oral intake and dehydration for at least one week. En route, his blood pressure was 94/49 mmHg, and he received 1 L of intravenous normal saline. On arrival, he was somnolent and oriented only to self. His vital signs were: temperature 37.1 °C, blood pressure 101/59 mmHg, heart rate 105 beats per minute, respiratory rate 17 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 100% on room air. Examination revealed a sarcopenic-appearing man with dry mucous membranes and no acute distress.

Initial laboratory results were notable for acute renal failure and severe metabolic acidosis: sodium 145 mEq/L, potassium 6.6 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 207 mg/dL, creatinine 10.2 mg/dL (baseline 1.1 mg/dL), glucose 185 mg/dL, chloride 106 mEq/L, bicarbonate 8 mEq/L, anion gap 31, venous pH 7.09, and lactate 4.4 mmol/L. A urinary catheter revealed trace ketones on repeat urinalysis. A β-hydroxybutyrate level was elevated at 31.5 mmol/L. High-sensitivity troponin levels were 213 ng/L at baseline, 223 ng/L at 1 hour, and 193 ng/L at 3 hours; electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm without ST-T changes. 

His home medications included insulin glargine 18 units nightly, insulin aspart 5 units before each meal, and empagliflozin started one month earlier.

A 48-year-old otherwise healthy woman presented with a 5-day history of headache, nausea, and vomiting. Physical examination and laboratory tests were within normal limits. She was diagnosed with tension headache and sinusitis and discharged on trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole. Three days later, her headache had resolved but vomiting persisted twice daily; she was treated with an over-the-counter proton pump inhibitor for suspected gastroesophageal reflux. Over the following week, she developed ataxia, diplopia, and recurrence of her headache. 

She presented to the emergency department, and a T2-weighted MRI of the head showed increased signaling of the left temporal lobe, bilateral pontine regions, left peridentate nucleus, and cervical spinal cord. These findings were thought to represent an acute demyelinating process. Clinical suspicion for myasthenia gravis was high, and she was administered a trial of pyridostigmine without improvement. During hospitalization, her blood pressure rose to 190/90 mmHg, serum sodium was 123 mEq/L, glucose 176 mg/dL, and white-cell count 12,800 cells/mL. Neurologically, she had decreased sensorium, hallucinations, diminished attention span, and gait disturbance. A lumbar puncture showed an elevated opening pressure. 

Based on radiographic, laboratory, and clinical findings, a diagnosis of acute demyelinating encephalopathy was made, and suspicions of infectious encephalitis, collagen vascular disease, and toxic encephalitis were high. She received plasmapheresis without improvement. A follow-up T2-weighted MRI showed progressive enlargement of the bilateral pontine regions with hydrocephalus and mass effect on the fourth ventricle. Because of the absence of pathological enhancement of the pons, this was felt to represent either an aggressive demyelinating process or a low-grade glioma. The patient continued to deteriorate, became comatose, and died approximately four weeks after admission.

A 25-year-old woman presented with a painless lump in the left cheek, first noted nine months earlier. She reported no toothache, numbness, or systemic symptoms and had no significant medical history. On examination, there was left facial asymmetry without skin changes. A 67‐year‐old man with a 3‐year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus managed with metformin, glimepiride, and a prior percutaneous coronary intervention for acute myocardial infarction 2 months earlier was referred for treatment of newly diagnosed extensive ulcerative colitis. Immunohistochemical staining of the fluid was positive for calretinin and weakly positive for CK5/6 and MOC31.

A 47-year-old man was referred for mechanical circulatory support for severe cardiogenic shock with multiorgan failure of unknown cause. One day earlier, he had undergone excision of a benign thyroglossal duct cyst, during which he experienced recurrent hypertensive episodes. After extubation, he developed profound hypotension and pulmonary oedema. Transthoracic echocardiography showed severely impaired left ventricular (LV) systolic function. Coronary angiography revealed no evidence of relevant coronary artery disease, and toxicological screening was negative. His medical history included chronic polyarthritis and treated arterial hypertension.

Blood pressure was 75/49 mmHg, heart rate 180 b.p.m., with bilateral rales and basal dullness on chest percussion. He experienced pulseless electrical activity requiring 5 minutes of resuscitation. Bedside echocardiography demonstrated akinesia of all basal and mid LV segments with preserved apical contraction (left ventricular ejection fraction, 15%); right ventricular function was preserved (TAPSE 17 mm). On the basis of these findings, reverse takotsubo cardiomyopathy was suspected. A percutaneous LV assist device (Impella CP®) was implanted immediately. Endomyocardial biopsy revealed moderate chronically active myocarditis with diffuse interstitial remodelling, and PCR testing showed no evidence of acute or persistent myocardial infection.

A 56-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a recurrent skin lesion on the dorsum of his right thumb. A 64-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of right upper abdominal pain without nausea, vomiting, chills, or fever. She had no history of hepatitis, surgery, or hereditary disease, and no underlying medical conditions. On examination, she was afebrile and oriented; there was right upper abdominal tenderness without rebound or palpable masses, no hepatosplenomegaly, and negative Murphy’s sign and shifting dullness.

Laboratory studies showed:  
• AFP 2.4 µg/l (normal 0.0–7.0)  
• CEA 11.6 µg/l (normal 0.0–5.0)  
• CA-125 32.3 KIU/l (normal 0.0–35.0)  
• CA19-9 228.0 KIU/l (normal 0.0–30.0)  
• Other liver enzymes and blood counts largely within reference ranges, except WBC 11.9×10^9/l (normal 3.5–9.5×10^9/l).

Ultrasonography revealed a heterogeneous echoic mass near the gallbladder fossa in the right liver lobe, calcifications in the right liver, multiple gallstones with gallbladder wall thickening, and enhanced pancreatic echogenicity. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a lesion in the right hepatic lobe adjacent to the gallbladder fossa, multiple enlarged hepatic hilar lymph nodes, and findings of gallstones with cholecystitis. Liver MRI demonstrated an occupying lesion in the right lobe with mild intrahepatic bile duct dilatation, raising the possibility of intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, along with gallstones and cholecystitis. No extrahepatic primary tumor was identified.

clinical_record:
A male newborn was referred at 1 day of age for cyanosis; oxygen saturation (SaO2) was 80% in room air. Laboratory findings showed a hematocrit of 47.8% and a platelet count of 103 000/mm3; other values were normal and there were no signs of infection. Echocardiography revealed pulmonary atresia with ventricular septal defect and a patent ductus arteriosus. A prostaglandin infusion was started, raising SaO2 to 90–95%. On day 11, he underwent a systemic‐to‐pulmonary shunt operation with graft placement and PDA division. Preoperative values on day 10 were hematocrit 38.9%, platelet count 173 000/mm3, and SaO2 95% on prostaglandin. Postoperatively, hematocrit was 52.1% and platelet count was 58 000/mm3; platelet count then increased without transfusion. By postoperative day 6, he was extubated with SaO2 80–85%, hematocrit 41.1%, and platelet count 123 000/mm3. He was discharged on postoperative day 13 with SaO2 85–87%, hematocrit 33.4%, and platelet count 225 000/mm3.

At 10 months of age, he was admitted for a Rastelli operation. His SaO2 was 80%; hematocrit was 49.1% and platelet count was 68 000/mm3. He had no bleeding history or medications. Prothrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time, and INR were normal; peripheral smear was unremarkable. Antiplatelet antibodies and platelet‐associated immunoglobulins were negative; antinuclear and anti–double‐stranded DNA antibodies were normal. Platelet aggregation time was 127 s (reference, 61–110 s). Viral and bacterial studies were insignificant. The pediatrician made a provisional diagnosis of immune thrombocytopenia and administered intravenous immunoglobulins (2 g/kg) the day before surgery. On the day of operation, hematocrit was 42.6% and platelet count was 77 000/mm3.

clinical_record:
A 44-year-old woman presented with a two-week history of abnormal behavior, decreased concentration, and postural instability. She had a history of insomnia and irritable bowel syndrome and was taking vitamin D3, vitamin K, manganese, and activated charcoal. She and her parents denied other medications. She had been started on lorazepam by her general practitioner without improvement.

On examination, vital signs were normal. Teeth had a greyish discoloration. Neurologic exam showed confusion, impaired attention, and disorientation. Muscle tone and strength were normal; coordination, sensation, and cranial nerves were intact; there were no pyramidal signs.

While in the emergency department, she became more somnolent and developed frequent myoclonic jerks. Laboratory tests including CBC, renal, hepatic, and thyroid function, CRP, vitamin B12, and folate were normal; syphilis and HIV tests were negative. Noncontrast brain CT was unremarkable. Lumbar puncture showed protein 47 mg/dL (15–45) and 10 WBC/μL (<5). Empiric IV acyclovir and ceftriaxone were started for possible infectious encephalitis.

On the neurology service, she remained moderately drowsy with exuberant generalized myoclonus at rest and on action. EEG revealed generalized background slowing without focal or periodic features. Brain MRI on hospital day 5 was normal. She clinically worsened despite antivirals and antibiotics, so intravenous immunoglobulin was given empirically for presumed autoimmune encephalitis. A trial of levetiracetam 1000 mg/day failed to improve the myoclonus.

reviewer_a.reason: Autoimmune encephalitis was considered and treated empirically, but the record does not confirm this diagnosis. It is a differential diagnosis or a presumed diagnosis, not a confirmed one.

clinical_record:
A 20-year-old unmarried girl, deaf and mute since birth, presented with a 6-month history of a slowly enlarging left vulvar swelling that had become extremely painful during the past week. She had no fever or vaginal discharge. On examination, her vital signs were stable and she was afebrile, with no inguinal lymphadenopathy. Local examination showed a left labial swelling with signs of inflammation, and a clinical diagnosis of Bartholin’s abscess was made; she was started on parenteral antibiotics. Within 24 hours, her pain decreased and the inflammation subsided. Because the patient and her parents insisted that she was sexually naïve, the lesion was reexamined. Now noted was a 5 × 5 cm swelling of the left labia majora without signs of inflammation; the mass was firm (not cystic), the labia minora were not everted, and the hymen was intact.

reviewer_b.missing_or_conflicting_component: leiomyoma-specific smooth muscle origin
reviewer_b.reason: Vulvar fibroma is a benign solid tumor in the differential but lacks the smooth muscle component of leiomyoma.

A 27-year-old man with a history of a 5 mm‐thick melanoma on his posterior neck treated six years earlier by wide local excision (no sentinel lymph node biopsy, no adjuvant therapy) presented with hemoptysis and dyspnea. Vital signs were within normal limits. Physical examination was notable only for scattered breath sounds without stridor. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were unremarkable.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed a 3.1 × 2.7 × 3.6 cm mass in the right lower lobe. Endobronchial ultrasound–guided fine-needle aspiration of the lung lesion demonstrated a malignant small round blue cell tumor. Molecular studies were negative for an EWSR1 translocation but otherwise were interpreted as consistent with Ewing sarcoma/primitive neuroectodermal tumor (PNET). 

Positron emission tomography (PET)/CT showed an FDG-avid right lower lobe mass and an intensely FDG-avid, partially calcified 4.1 × 2.3 × 2.8 cm expansile lesion within the right hyoid bone. Ultrasound–guided core needle biopsy of the hyoid lesion was nondiagnostic, yielding only rare atypical epithelial cells amidst lymphocytes.

An 18-year-old Chinese woman noted a grey dot in the central vision of her left eye 4 days before presentation. Magnetic resonance angiography of the brain was normal. A 32-year-old Han Chinese man, a professional driver, presented with a 4-year history of a slowly enlarging pigmented lesion on the upper left lip vermilion. He first noticed a 1 cm × 0.5 cm macule, which progressively increased in size without symptoms. After 3 years, he noted brownish discoloration of the skin above the vermilion. A 28-year-old Hispanic man with a history of alcoholic cirrhosis presented with a 10-day history of a pruritic eruption that began on the trunk and gradually spread to all extremities. He denied contact allergens, fever, or hyperhidrosis and had no prior history of atopic dermatitis, dermatophytosis, or hand eczema. On examination, he had scleral icterus and multiple dusky, thin plaques with a central collarette of scale on the face, neck, axillae, trunk, and extremities. On both hands and feet, there were hyperkeratotic plaques and deeply seated vesicles with a greenish-black hue, especially accentuated along the dermatoglyphic ridges. Laboratory testing showed total bilirubin 28.9 mg/dL (reference <1.2), direct bilirubin 17.7 mg/dL (<0.3), AST 78 IU/L, ALT 42 IU/L, and alkaline phosphatase 231 IU/L. A punch biopsy of the right palm revealed psoriasiform epidermal acanthosis, intraepidermal spongiosis, hyperkeratosis with sparse perivascular lymphocytic inflammation, and a dilated eccrine duct containing amorphous pink material. Gram, periodic acid–Schiff, and iron stains were negative. Punch biopsies of the chest and thigh were consistent with pityriasis rosea.

A 10-day-old, 40-kg male Chianina calf was referred for evaluation of progressive dyspnea, lethargy, and recumbency. On presentation, temperature was 38.5 °C; heart rate, 170 beats/min with regular rhythm; respiratory rate, 60 breaths/min; jugular pulses were present and mucous membranes were cyanotic, especially after brief exertion. Cardiac auscultation revealed a grade IV/VI right apical systolic murmur and a more pronounced heartbeat on the right precordium. Lung sounds were harsh bronchovesicular. Electrocardiography showed sinus tachycardia at 170 beats/min. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated severe dilation of the right atrium and right ventricle, a markedly hypoplastic left ventricle with a severely reduced mitral valve orifice, a 16 mm interatrial defect in the upper septum, and a 6 mm muscular interventricular defect in the dorsal septum. An oblique parasternal long-axis view revealed two great vessels arising in parallel from the right ventricle, differentiated by coronary arteries from one vessel and by left and right pulmonary arteries from the other. Color-flow Doppler showed severe tricuspid regurgitation and bidirectional shunting at both septal defects. Agitated saline contrast injected via the left jugular vein produced bubbles in the left atrium and ventricle and exiting the right ventricle through both great vessels.

A 48-year-old man with a 12-year history of perianal fistula presented with recent mucinous discharge, pain, and perianal induration. One year earlier, he had undergone incision and drainage of a recurrent perianal abscess.

clinical_record:
A 30-year-old gravida 2, para 1 woman was referred at 32 weeks’ gestation after an abnormal routine ultrasound. She had no significant medical history, no medication use, and no history of trauma. Previous prenatal care had been irregular.  
Transabdominal ultrasound showed bilateral ventriculomegaly with dilation of both frontal and occipital horns, irregular ventricular walls, multiple hyperechoic regions with indistinct margins within the ventricular lumens, and a roughened-appearing choroid plexus.  
Fetal Doppler ultrasound demonstrated normal middle cerebral artery perfusion.  
Fetal MRI confirmed bilateral ventricular enlargement and identified areas of high signal intensity on T1-weighted images and low signal intensity on T2-weighted images within the ventricles.  
A comprehensive workup—including a TORCH panel, platelet count, prothrombin time, partial thromboplastin time, plasminogen levels, von Willebrand factor, factor V Leiden, protein S, protein C, and antiplatelet antibodies—returned within normal limits.

reviewer_a.reason: The record describes ventriculomegaly in a fetus, which is inherently congenital. The candidate is a compatible child of the broader 'Fetal ventriculomegaly' but adds the 'Congenital' specifier which is implied by the fetal context.

reviewer_b.missing_or_conflicting_component: hemorrhage
reviewer_b.reason: Ventriculomegaly is a broader finding that can result from hemorrhage, but the candidate does not specify the hemorrhage etiology.

A 23-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of progressive abdominal distension accompanied by early satiety and urinary urgency. She denied pain, weight loss, or systemic symptoms. Her menstrual cycles were normal, and her mother had a history of ovarian cysts. On examination, the abdomen was distended with dull percussion notes but without tenderness or guarding.

Transabdominal ultrasonography revealed a cyst measuring 16 × 24 cm that compressed adjacent abdominal organs. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography showed a large midline intraperitoneal cyst, 30 × 25.6 × 16.8 cm in size, extending from the liver to the pelvis and involving the uterus and ovaries. The lesion had a fluid density of 20 Hounsfield units and demonstrated no calcifications, soft-tissue components, or enhancing septations, suggesting a benign etiology.

Laboratory studies, including α-fetoprotein, carcinoembryonic antigen, cancer antigen 19-9, and cancer antigen 125, were all within normal limits; the Risk of Malignancy Algorithm (ROMA) score was 4.1 %. Serological testing for Echinococcus granulosus was negative. A giant intra-abdominal cyst was diagnosed preoperatively, and laparoscopic cyst aspiration with exploration under general anesthesia was planned.

A 44-year-old woman presented with a 4-month history of severe occipital and temporal headaches that were paroxysmal, aggravated by changes in position, and associated with bilateral blurry vision and morning projectile vomiting. Routine blood tests were unremarkable.
